title: Take the allergy seriously — write it down
instruction: Ask what they're allergic to and how severe, and put it on the ticket.
rationale: An allergy told out loud and never written down survives exactly as long as it takes for the ticket to change hands. The ticket is what every set of hands behind this bar actually reads before a bottle gets touched.

title: Check the bottles for hidden nuts
instruction: Walk the back bar and identify every nut liqueur before you touch a shaker.
rationale: Nothing on this menu says almond or hazelnut anywhere in its name, so the bottle's own label — not the recipe committed to memory — is what a nut allergy actually depends on getting right.

title: Check the house syrup's recipe card
instruction: Read what's actually in the house-made syrup before it goes anywhere near this order.
rationale: A house-made syrup carries no label of its own — the recipe card kept behind the bar is the only place its egg white, dairy, or nut content is written down at all, which is exactly why it gets checked instead of assumed.

title: Pull dedicated tools for this order
instruction: A jigger that hasn't measured a nut liqueur tonight, then a shaker straight off the clean rack.
rationale: Cross-contact travels through the tool as much as the ingredient — a jigger or shaker that measured amaretto an hour ago carries enough residue to matter to a real allergy, so this order gets equipment nothing else has touched tonight.

title: Pour the nut-free substitute
instruction: Carry the nut-free syrup to the clean shaker — not the orgeat, not the amaretto.
rationale: The substitute only protects anyone once it is actually the thing that goes in the shaker. Deciding to use it and then reaching for the familiar bottle out of habit is the same mistake as never deciding at all.

title: Shake it in the clean shaker
instruction: Hold the shake — this glass never touches the tools that made the last round.
rationale: The shake itself is the last chance for cross-contact to happen unnoticed, so it happens in the tool that has touched nothing else tonight, held the full count rather than rushed to get to the next ticket.

title: Strain, garnish safe, and mark it
instruction: Strain into a clean glass and mark the ticket so the kitchen and the next bartender both know why.
rationale: A correctly made allergy drink that arrives at the table unmarked is one glass swap away from being the wrong drink to the wrong guest — the mark on the ticket is what keeps the whole chain honest after it leaves your hands.

title: Take the non-alcoholic order at face value
instruction: No follow-up questions about why — just build it right.
rationale: A guest who orders non-alcoholic is owed the same care as anyone else's order, not a raised eyebrow or a second guess about the reason. "Mocktail" is a drink order, not a conversation starter.

title: Build the mocktail to the recipe
instruction: Steady build — the same care as any other ticket, not a rushed afterthought.
rationale: A mocktail thrown together fast because it "doesn't really count" reads to the guest exactly like what it is. Building it at the same steady pace as anything else on the rail is the whole of what taking it seriously looks like.

title: Mark the glass so it can't be mistaken
instruction: A flag straw or a marked ticket — something that survives the glass changing hands.
rationale: A mocktail that looks identical to the drink beside it is a swap waiting to happen the first time a runner, a friend, or a second bartender touches the tray. The mark is what keeps a non-alcoholic order non-alcoholic after it leaves your sight.

title: Check the garnish tray
instruction: Tongs, not fingers — and check what's actually preserving that dried fruit.
rationale: A shared garnish tray is a cross-contact surface like any cutting board, and the fruit sitting on it can carry its own disclosure requirement. Both get the same attention the bottles already got.

title: Swap the beer for a celiac guest
instruction: Barley and wheat mean gluten — pour the gluten-free alternative instead.
rationale: Beer is made from barley or wheat and carries gluten that no tap handle discloses on its own. A guest who says celiac gets the gluten-free cider or spirit poured without having to ask twice.

title: Read the sulphite disclosure on the wine
instruction: "Contains Sulfites" is required on the label for a reason — read it before you pour for a sensitive guest.
rationale: The TTB requires a sulphite disclosure on any wine carrying ten parts per million or more, which makes the label — not the varietal, not the producer's reputation — the actual answer for a guest who reacts to sulphites.

title: Someone starts reacting — respond in order
instruction: Hives are spreading at the rail. Find their auto-injector, call 911, and keep them from walking out.
rationale: Most guests who carry a serious allergy carry their own auto-injector, and finding it fast is the one action that can reverse a closing airway before EMS arrives. The call follows immediately after, and nobody lets a reacting guest walk out to their car alone while any of this is happening — and OSHA's 1910.1030 bloodborne pathogen standard is why the used needle goes to EMS or a sharps container, never a bare hand or the trash.

title: Log what was served and what happened
instruction: Write down the drink, the ingredient, the timeline and the outcome once EMS has the guest.
rationale: A written record of exactly what was in the glass and when the reaction started is what the receiving hospital and the venue's own review both need afterward — and it is what proves the protocol was followed rather than just believed to have been.

situation: A colleague hands you a fresh shaker for the next round — it's still wet with orgeat from the last ticket.
instruction: Swap it for a clean one before this order goes anywhere near it.
missed: The allergy order went into the shaker your colleague handed you. It had already held orgeat that shift, and "rinsed" is not the same claim as "clean" for someone whose reaction does not care about the difference.

situation: A friend at the table has ordered a shot "as a joke" and is sliding it toward the guest who ordered non-alcoholic.
instruction: Intercept the shot before it reaches them.
missed: The shot reached the table. A non-alcoholic order that ends up with alcohol in it anyway — pushed there by a third party — is exactly the failure this whole request was trying to avoid, and it happened while you were watching.

explanation: You poured from the amaretto bottle itself. Amaretto is an almond-flavoured liqueur and one of the most common hidden nut sources behind a bar — reaching for the familiar bottle instead of the nut-free substitute is exactly the mistake this whole check exists to catch.

You dressed the glass with bare hands instead of the tongs. A garnish tray is touched by every drink that crosses it, and a bare hand carries whatever the last five drinks left on it straight onto a glass somebody said they cannot safely touch.

You reached for the shaker already sitting on the rail instead of a clean one. It shook a regular round twenty minutes ago and carries enough residue on the gasket to matter to a true allergy — an allergy order gets its own clean tool every time, not whichever one is closest.

You poured from the house lager tap for a customer who said celiac. Beer is made from barley or wheat and carries gluten the label on the tap handle never mentions — the gluten-free alternative is the pour, not the lager with a splash of something else in it.

title: Read the ticket's allergen flag
instruction: Check the ticket on the rail for the allergen icon before touching anything.
rationale: The flag on the ticket is the only thing standing between an ordinary dish and one that has to be built completely differently — missing it here means every step after this one is being done for the wrong dish.

title: Call the order back to the expediter
instruction: Repeat the allergen and the table back to the expo before starting the dish.
rationale: ServSafe's allergen training calls for a verbal read-back for exactly this order type, because a ticket read silently can be misread silently — saying it out loud and having the expo confirm it catches a wrong table, a wrong allergen or a wrong dish before a single pan gets pulled.

title: Pull the dedicated purple board
instruction: Take the purple allergen board off the rack, not any of the coloured line boards.
rationale: The purple board exists so an allergen order is visually distinct from across the kitchen, not just correctly prepared up close — anyone glancing at the line can see this board is doing different work, which is the whole point of colour coding under pressure.

title: Pull the dedicated knife and pan
instruction: Take the dedicated knife and pan kept separate from the shared line equipment.
rationale: A knife or pan that has touched the allergen even once today carries it into whatever it touches next — the dedicated set is kept apart from the shared line specifically so this order never has to trust that a shared tool happens to be clean enough.

title: Wash hands before touching the order
instruction: Wash hands fully before the allergen ingredients come out.
rationale: Whatever the last thing your hands touched was is now on this dish unless it's washed off first — the handwash resets the one tool you can't swap out for a dedicated one.

title: Change gloves
instruction: Pull a fresh pair of gloves after the handwash.
rationale: Gloves worn on the rest of the line have touched whatever the rest of the line has touched — a fresh pair after the wash is the second half of the same reset, not a redundant one.

title: Check the mise against the recipe's allergen list
instruction: Compare every ingredient staged for this dish against the recipe's own allergen list before cooking starts.
rationale: FALCPA's eight allergens plus sesame under the FASTER Act cover milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame — nine names a recipe's own allergen list has to be checked against ingredient by ingredient, because a sauce or a garnish can carry one of them without looking any different from the version that doesn't.

title: Move to the dedicated station
instruction: Carry the dedicated pan to the clean station away from the shared line and the shared fryer.
rationale: Standing at the shared line to cook a dedicated pan puts it back in splash and steam range of everything the rest of the line is doing — the dedicated station exists so distance, not just dedicated equipment, is doing part of the work.

title: Cook on the dedicated burner
instruction: Hold a steady cook on the dedicated pan and burner.
rationale: The dedicated pan only protects the order for as long as it stays on the dedicated burner — set it down on a shared burner for even a minute and whatever that burner's grate has on it is now underneath this dish too.

title: Mark the plate
instruction: Plate the dish, then set the allergen marker on it before it leaves the station.
rationale: The marker is what tells the expediter and the server, at a glance, that this specific plate needs the care the ticket called for — a correctly built dish with no marker on it is indistinguishable from an ordinary one the moment it leaves your hands.

title: Walk the plate to the pass yourself
instruction: Carry the finished plate to the pass personally rather than handing it to someone else.
rationale: Handing an allergen plate to somebody else to run is one more point where it can get set down next to the wrong dish or picked up by the wrong runner — the cook who built it walking it to the pass is the last checkpoint the ticket gets before a server ever touches it.

title: Sanitise and return the dedicated tools
instruction: Clean the dedicated board, knife and pan and return them to allergen storage, separate from the line's own tools.
rationale: The dedicated set only stays trustworthy for the next allergen ticket if it goes back to its own storage clean — left on the line rack even once, it's one more shared tool the next cook has no reason to think is any different.

situation: The cook next to you, moving fast, reaches for your dedicated pan with the spatula he's been using on the shared line all night.
instruction: Get your own dedicated utensil into that pan before his does.
missed: The shared spatula went into the dedicated pan before anyone stopped it, and every ingredient the rest of the line has touched tonight is now a contact on this specific plate.

situation: The expediter calls back across the pass — table 12's dish, already plated and sitting under the heat lamp, has a walnut flag on its ticket that nobody caught until now.
instruction: Pull that plate before it leaves the pass.
missed: The plate went out to table 12 with an allergen nobody flagged in time to stop it, which is the one outcome every step before this one was built to make impossible.

explanation: That's a shared cutting board off the line rack, not the dedicated purple one. Whatever the last thing cut on it was is now a residue on a board about to touch an allergen order — colour coding only works if the allergen order actually uses the board it's colour-coded for.

That's the shared fryer basket — the same oil every other order on the line goes through today, tree nuts and shellfish breading included. Frying an allergen order's own ingredients in shared oil is a contact with every allergen that has gone through that oil this shift, full stop, no matter how clean the ingredients going in are.

That garnish bin is the shared one every station on the line dips into, and a shared spoon just went from a plate with tree nuts on it straight into this bin. An allergen order's own plate can be perfect and still pick up a contact from the garnish that goes on last.

You're about to start cooking without ever calling the ticket back to the expediter. The callback is what catches a flag that got missed reading the ticket the first time — skip it and the only check left is whatever happens to be right the first time through.

title: Read the batch card
instruction: Check the bowl size, the attachment, the starting speed and the mix time.
rationale: The card sets the attachment and the starting speed before the bowl ever goes up — a bread dough hook run at a whisk's speed tears the gluten instead of building it, and that's a wasted batch discovered only after the timer runs out.

title: Prove the bowl guard interlock
instruction: Hold the guard open through the full check and confirm the beater stops dead, not coasts.
rationale: OSHA 1910.212 exists for exactly this machine: the guard is the safeguard, and a safeguard that hasn't been tested today is an assumption wearing a guard's shape. Proving it stops the beater the instant it lifts is what makes everything that follows — the chute, the scrape-down — actually safe to do the way the procedure says.

title: Raise the bowl on the lift
instruction: Turn the lift crank until the bowl reaches mixing height.
rationale: The lift carries the bowl's full weight plus whatever's in it, which is exactly why it's a geared crank and not a lift by hand — a 60-quart bowl of dough is not something anybody's back should be finding out the hard way.

title: Seat the lift lock
instruction: Hold the lock pin engaged until it seats fully at mixing height.
rationale: A bowl held up by the crank alone can settle the moment anyone leans on it; the lock pin is what actually keeps it at height under load. It has to be held through the full seat, not bumped and let go, or the lock can catch on the first tooth instead of the last one.

title: Seat the attachment on the spindle
instruction: Lift the attachment from the rack and seat it square on the spindle.
rationale: The card named this attachment for a reason — a hook builds gluten, a paddle creams fat and sugar, and the wrong one on the spindle either tears the dough or never actually creams the batch, whatever the timer says.

title: Pin the attachment
instruction: Lock the retaining pin so the attachment can't walk off the spindle.
rationale: Nothing about the spindle stops an unpinned attachment from working its way upward under load — the pin is the only thing holding it down there, and it gets checked before the mixer ever starts turning, not after something sounds wrong.

title: Set the starting speed from the card
instruction: Bring the speed dial to the card's starting figure and commit inside the band.
rationale: A mixer only changes speed safely at a stop — this dial gets set once, from the card, before the start switch is ever touched, because reaching for it once the beater is already loaded and turning is how a hand ends up at the edge of a moving bowl.

title: Add ingredients through the guard's chute
instruction: Carry the flour bag to the chute opening and feed it through — never over the top of the guard.
rationale: The chute is the one gap this guard has, sized for a stream of flour and nothing wider than that. Dumping over the guard instead puts a hand exactly where the guard's whole job is to keep it from being.

title: Run the batch to the card's time
instruction: Hold the start switch through the mix time on the card.
rationale: A mixer left running past its own timer overworks the dough the same way an early stop underworks it — the card's time is the target because somebody already found out what happens on either side of it.

title: Stop the mixer before scraping down
instruction: Hit the stop switch fully before the guard or the scraper comes anywhere near the bowl.
rationale: This is the one action that makes the next step legal at all — the beater has to be stopped, not slowing, before the guard opens. A mixer that's still coasting down is still a mixer with a moving beater in it.

title: Scrape the bowl down
instruction: Open the guard and run the scraper along the bowl wall in steady, controlled strokes.
rationale: The scrape-down only happens stopped and guard open — the flip side of the rule that keeps the guard closed while the beater turns. A controlled pass along the wall gets the unmixed edges back into the batch without a hand anywhere near a beater that's still capable of moving.

title: Lower the bowl off the lift
instruction: Release the lock and turn the crank to bring the finished batch back down.
rationale: The bowl comes down the same controlled way it went up — geared, not dropped — because a full 60-quart bowl let go of partway down the crank is exactly the weight the lift exists to manage in the first place.

title: Lock out the mixer for the deep clean
instruction: Turn the main power off and apply your lock before the guard or the bowl seal comes apart for cleaning.
rationale: A between-batch scrape happens stopped; a full teardown for the deep clean happens locked out — OSHA 1910.147, the same control of hazardous energy a machine shop uses on a press brake, sized here for a mixer somebody is about to reach fully inside of.

title: Walk the station before the next batch
instruction: Two things at this mixer are wrong. Find them by looking.
rationale: A guard that still closes and a spindle that still spins are not the same as a mixer that's actually ready for the next baker — the two things worth catching now are exactly the ones nobody notices until the batch after this one.

situation: Another baker has grabbed a scraper and is reaching straight for the bowl — the beater is still turning and they don't see it.
instruction: There's a hand headed for a moving beater and the mixer is still running.
missed: The reach happened anyway while the beater kept turning. A 60-quart hook does not stop for a hand that gets there first — the switch has to beat the reach, not follow it.

situation: You feel the bowl lift's lock give a notch — the bowl has started to settle while the guard is still open and your hands are on the scraper.
instruction: The bowl underneath your hands is drifting down on its own.
missed: The bowl kept settling with the lock unseated and your hand still at the rim. It happened to stop before it caught anything. A lift lock that's given once is a lift lock that gives again — it gets reseated the moment it's felt, not after the stroke you're mid-way through.

explanation: That spare beater on the shelf has no retaining pin fitted. An attachment that isn't pinned to the spindle can walk up and off under load, and thirty pounds of steel coming off a spinning shaft doesn't announce which direction it's going first.

You went to dump that bag straight over the top of the guard instead of through its chute. The chute is the only opening in this guard for a reason — pouring around it means your hand follows the bag right up to the edge the guard exists to keep it away from.

The guard on this mixer is propped open with a wedge instead of resting on its own interlock. A wedged guard can't do the one thing it's there for — stop the machine the instant it lifts — so reaching through it is reaching into a bowl the interlock was never actually watching.

You brought the scraper to the bowl while the beater was still turning. A 60-quart hook has enough torque to take a scraper — and the hand holding it — around with the dough. The bowl gets scraped stopped, guard open, every time, not while it's still moving.

title: Read the event order
instruction: Check the guest count, the menu, plated or buffet service, and the room's timeline.
rationale: The event order sets everything downstream: how many hot boxes you load, how long the buffet has to hold before the room is cleared, and whether tonight is a plated service with a cart call or a buffet with a two-hour recheck clock. Walking onto a banquet line without reading it first means guessing at numbers a banquet captain already wrote down for you.

title: Preheat the hot box
instruction: Turn the hot box thermostat up to operating temperature before anything goes in it.
rationale: A hot box holds food at temperature, it does not bring cold food up to it, and loading pans into a cabinet that has not come up to heat starts every one of them in the danger zone at once. Preheating first means the cabinet is doing its job the moment the first pan lands on the rack instead of racing to catch up with forty covers already inside it.

title: Confirm the hot box is holding
instruction: Probe the empty cabinet's air temperature through the port and commit once it is holding in range.
rationale: The dial tells you where the thermostat is set, not what the cabinet is actually doing — a door seal going soft or a fan motor dying shows up as a hot box that runs cooler than its own dial claims. The probe through the port is the only number in this room that checks the machine rather than trusting it.

title: Load the hot box
instruction: Carry the finished pan from the prep table into the preheated hot box.
rationale: Product goes from the range or the oven straight into a cabinet that is already holding temperature — parked on a cart in the hallway on the way there is time in the danger zone that never gets logged and never gets back. The hot box is the only stop this pan makes before the buffet.

title: Probe the pan before it goes out
instruction: Probe the pan on the buffet and commit only once it reads 135°F or above.
rationale: Every pan gets probed on its way to the guest, not on its way out of the kitchen — travel time, an elevator ride, a service door propped open, all cost temperature between the two. 135°F is the Food Code's hot-holding floor, and the only pan that has actually met it is the one you probed where the guest is about to be served from.

title: Light the chafer lid open
instruction: Open the chafer's lid first, then light the fuel can underneath it.
rationale: Fuel gel gives off vapour the second the lid comes off the can, and lighting it under a closed chafer lid traps that vapour until somebody lifts the lid — the flare that follows goes straight up into whoever's hands are on it. Open first, light second, every chafer, every time.

title: Set the flame regulator
instruction: Hold the fuel can's fold-cap regulator in the band that keeps the flame steady, not smothered and not flaring.
rationale: Chafing fuel's fold-cap is the only control you have over how hard it burns once it is lit: folded too far closed and the pan runs cold before the entrée does; open too wide and the flame reaches high enough to catch a sleeve or a napkin passed too close over it. The band in the middle is the one that holds 135°F without becoming the thing a guest points at.

title: Walk the buffet before doors open
instruction: Three things on this buffet are not right. Find them before the first guest comes through.
rationale: The buffet is checked with your own eyes and a hand on the guard before service, because a gap or a mis-rested utensil found mid-service means every guest ahead of that moment was served past it. This is the last look you get at the line the way the room is about to see it.

title: Time-tag the dinner rolls
instruction: Write the discard time and attach the tag to the bread basket held on time, not temperature.
rationale: Bread is not hot-held and it is not refrigerated on the buffet — it is controlled under Time as a Public Health Control, which the Food Code allows only when the item is marked with the time it has to be discarded by. No tag on the basket means nobody downstream of you knows it is even under time control at all.

title: Hold the two-hour recheck
instruction: Probe the buffet pan again at the two-hour mark and hold for the full reading.
rationale: A pan that was 145°F when the doors opened can be under 135°F two hours later with nothing about it looking different from across the room — the steam is the same, the pan looks the same, and the only thing that has changed is the one thing you cannot see. The recheck is what catches a pan drifting out of hold before a guest does.

title: Cover the plated meals
instruction: Take a dome from the stack and cover every plate on the cart.
rationale: A plated course loses heat the moment it leaves the kitchen, and the dome is the only thing slowing that down between the pass and the table. An uncovered plate on a cart crossing a ballroom floor arrives at the guest's seat colder than the kitchen ever sent it out.

title: Call the corners on the cart
instruction: Push the cart through the service door calling front, then left, then right as each corner clears.
rationale: A loaded banquet cart is wider than the person pushing it and blind past the first row of domes, and the call is for whoever is on the other side of that door as much as for you — front first because that is the corner about to meet a doorway, left and right as the cart swings clear of the frame behind it.

title: Cool the pull-down in a shallow ice bath
instruction: Move the leftover pan into a shallow container set in the ice bath rather than a deep one on the shelf.
rationale: A deep pan of hot food cools from the outside in and can sit in the danger zone for hours at its centre; a shallow pan in an ice bath brings the whole depth of the food down together. The Food Code's cooling window exists because a stockpot left to cool on a shelf overnight is a textbook case, not a hypothetical one.

title: Close out the pull-down log
instruction: Record what was cooled, what was discarded on its time tag, and sign the log closed.
rationale: The log is what turns tonight's pull-down into something the next shift can trust rather than something they have to guess at — what got a second life in tomorrow's prep, what hit its discard time and went in the bin, and whose signature is on that decision if anybody ever has to ask.

situation: A server flags the end pan on the buffet — it's reading 120°F on their own probe, well under hold.
instruction: That pan does not sit there while you finish something else.
missed: The pan sat there through the next course. A guest served from a 120°F pan has no way of knowing it fell out of hold, which is exactly why the check is the cook's job and not theirs.

situation: A runner has grabbed a fresh can of chafing fuel and is about to unscrew a lit chafer's spent can to swap it.
instruction: That can is still burning. Stop them before the cap comes off.
missed: The runner cracked the cap on a can that was still lit. Gel fuel vapour ignites off the flame it is sitting next to, and what should have been a routine swap becomes a fire on a table full of guests.

explanation: A bare hand in a hot chafer pan is a burn risk on a food already at serving temperature and a contamination risk on food nobody is cooking again — tongs and the plating spoon are on the rest six inches away for exactly this reach.

That tag's discard time passed eleven minutes ago and the pan is still on the buffet. Time as a Public Health Control only works if the tag is honoured — a pan held on time past its own deadline is being held on nothing.

That hot box door has been wedged open. A hot-holding cabinet loses its air temperature in minutes with the door open, and every pan inside starts falling through the danger zone together instead of one at a time on the line where you can see it happening.

That chafer's lid is still down and somebody left a lighter next to it. Lighting fuel under a closed lid traps the vapour it gives off while it catches, and the flare when the lid finally comes up reaches whoever is standing in front of it — the fuel is always lit with the lid open.

title: Read tonight's floor plan
instruction: Check the room diagram: table count, the dance floor's footprint, and where the risers and the aisles go.
rationale: Every table position, every aisle width and every riser placement in this room comes off a diagram somebody already worked out against the fire code's egress numbers — building the room from memory or from last week's layout is how an aisle that's supposed to stay four feet wide quietly becomes three.

title: Move the round table on the dolly
instruction: Carry the round table on the dolly to its marked spot on the floor plan.
rationale: The dolly carries the table's weight across the room so the two-person lift only has to happen once, at the very end, setting the table down onto its marked spot — rolled the whole distance instead of carried or dragged, it arrives at the lift with nobody's back already tired from getting it there.

title: Call the lift and hold it together
instruction: Call the lift with your partner and hold the table level between you until it's actually down.
rationale: A two-person lift only protects two backs when both people actually lift and lower on the same count — calling it out loud and holding the table level for the full count down is what turns 'ready' into an actual shared lift instead of one person taking the weight early while the other is still getting a grip, which is when the load ends up on one back instead of two.

title: Lock the table's legs down
instruction: Once the table is down and level, lock the legs.
rationale: Locking the legs before the table is actually down and level just means locking them onto a table that's about to move again — the lock goes on only once both of you have set the table down together, not while it's still being lowered.

title: Lift the chair stack with your knees, not your back
instruction: Bend at the knees before you grip the stack, then lift with your back straight.
rationale: A chair stack isn't heavy enough on its own to hurt anybody in one lift — it's the same bent-back reach repeated across two hundred chairs in a shift that turns into a strain, and the knees-first technique is the one thing standing between tonight's setup and next week's light-duty schedule.

title: Read the chair stack's height before adding to it
instruction: Watch the stack-height gauge climb as chairs go on and commit once it holds inside the safe limit.
rationale: Every stackable banquet chair carries a manufacturer's stated stacking limit for a reason that has nothing to do with the chairs themselves — past it, the column's own centre of gravity is what tips it, not anything anyone did wrong to it, and the gauge is the only thing on this floor that actually counts instead of eyeballing 'about right.'

title: Roll the finished stack to storage
instruction: Carry the stacked chairs from the floor to the storage cart.
rationale: A stack this tall carried by hand across an open floor blocks the one arm that would otherwise catch a stumble — the cart takes the height and the weight so the stack travels the same way it was built: under control, not balanced against a shoulder.

title: Align and lock the dance floor panels
instruction: Align the next panel against the one already down, then engage its latch.
rationale: An aligned panel that isn't latched is a trip edge waiting for the first dancer's heel to find it, and a latched panel that wasn't aligned first locks a step into the floor that stays there until somebody unlocks the whole run to fix it — the order is what keeps the floor flat instead of fast.

title: Square the riser section against the stage deck
instruction: Push the riser section flush against the deck before locking its legs.
rationale: A riser locked while it's still sitting at an angle to the deck next to it locks in a step between the two surfaces — squaring it first is what makes the lock actually produce a flat stage instead of a flat stage with a lip in the middle of it.

title: Engage the riser's leg-lock lever
instruction: Turn the leg-lock lever through to its stop.
rationale: The lock lever is what keeps a riser leg from folding or sliding once real weight — a performer, a speaker's podium, an amplifier stack — is actually standing on the platform, and it does that job only when it's thrown all the way to its stop, not partway.

title: Brace the platform while the lock sets
instruction: Keep a hand on the platform and hold it steady while the lock lever seats.
rationale: A leg-lock lever can bind partway through its throw on a platform that's still shifting under it, and holding the platform steady for the full few seconds it takes to seat is what turns 'the lever moved' into 'the leg is actually locked' — letting go early is how a lock that looks engaged turns out not to be, the first time weight lands on it.

title: Ramp the power run across the crew aisle
instruction: Set the cable ramp over the cord where it crosses the main aisle.
rationale: A cord run across an aisle a whole setup crew keeps crossing all night is a trip hazard with a schedule — the ramp is what turns a bare cord into a surface a foot can land on safely, and it goes on before the first person walks that aisle again, not after somebody already goes down.

title: Walk the aisles and the exits before doors open
instruction: Two things in this room are narrower or blocked compared to the plan. Find them before the room fills.
rationale: NFPA 101's egress requirements are only as real as the room actually measures on the night — a plan drawn with the right aisle widths and exit clearances protects nobody if the finished room has quietly drifted away from it by the time the doors open.

title: Log the changeover's time
instruction: Mark the room complete and the changeover time on the crew sheet.
rationale: The time sheet is what the union contract's setup-crew staffing language actually runs on — a changeover logged honestly is the record that shows whether tonight's room, at tonight's table count, was built with the crew and the time the contract calls for.

situation: Just as you and your partner are setting your own table down, a coworker across the room has picked up a round table by one edge and is trying to carry it alone rather than waiting for a second set of hands.
instruction: Grab the other side and lift it with them — don't let them keep carrying it solo.
missed: The table stayed a one-person carry the whole window. An off-balance table carried alone is a dropped table waiting on the first uneven spot in the floor, and nobody stepped in to make it a two-person lift before that happened.

situation: While you're bracing this platform, a second riser section nearby flexes underfoot as gear is loaded onto the stage — its leg-lock lever was never thrown and that platform is shifting.
instruction: Get the weight off it and throw the lock lever now.
missed: The section kept flexing under load with the lever never thrown. A riser leg that isn't locked doesn't announce it's about to fail — the flex was the only warning this platform gave, and it went unanswered.

explanation: That stack is already past the manufacturer's own stacking limit and leaning on the one behind it. Adding one more chair to a stack that's already top-heavy is how the whole column goes over — onto a floor a crew is still walking back and forth across.

That power run crosses the main crew aisle with nothing over it. OSHA's walking-working surfaces standard treats a bare cord across a walkway as a trip hazard the moment it's laid there, not the moment somebody actually catches a foot on it — every cord that crosses a path this room's own crew keeps walking gets a ramp, not an exception.

That table got dragged into position by one corner instead of carried by two people. Dragging a round table across a finished dance floor gouges the surface and puts the full weight on whoever's dragging it at a bad angle — the two-person lift exists so the table travels flat and the floor underneath it stays the floor the room paid to have refinished.

Wedging a shim under the riser leg instead of engaging the lock lever holds the platform level right up until weight actually lands on it. The lock is what keeps the section from shifting once a performer or a piece of gear is standing on it — a wedge is a guess dressed up to look like a fix.

title: Confirm the ABC licence and RBS certificates are posted
instruction: Check the wall board: the ABC licence current, and every RBS certificate on file for tonight's crew.
rationale: California has required RBS certification for anyone serving alcohol since 2022, and the ABC licence is what makes the whole night's service legal in the first place — both are checked posted and current before anything else, because an inspector or the county Environmental Health department can ask for either at any time.

title: Mix the sanitiser bucket to CalCode strength
instruction: Dip the test strip and read it against the colour card — commit once it lands in the required band.
rationale: The California Retail Food Code sets a working-strength range for the quaternary sanitiser every bar rag and glass gets wrung through all night — too weak and it does nothing, too strong and it is its own hazard under Cal/OSHA hazard communication rules, so the bucket is tested rather than guessed at from the bottle's own label.

title: Stock the hand sink
instruction: Soap, paper towels and the posted hand-washing sign — the hand sink is its own station, separate from the well.
rationale: The California Retail Food Code requires a dedicated hand sink stocked and posted before service, kept apart from the ice and glassware — a bartender who cannot wash their hands at an actual hand sink ends up doing it in the same basin the ice scoop sits next to, which is the exact cross-contamination the separate sink exists to prevent.

title: Burn out the ice well
instruction: Hold the hot-water flush on the empty well until it runs clean.
rationale: Yesterday's melt and whatever settled to the bottom of the well overnight get flushed out with hot water before any new ice goes in — the Retail Food Code treats an ice bin the same as any other food-contact surface, and an NSF-certified well is only as clean as the last time somebody actually flushed it rather than just refilling on top of what was already there.

title: Refill the well with the scoop — never a glass
instruction: Carry the fresh ice bag to the well and empty it in.
rationale: A scoop is a dedicated food-contact tool that never touches a customer's hand or mouth; a glass has been in both, and a cracked one left in the ice is a shard nobody sees until it is in somebody's drink. The Retail Food Code's rule against scooping ice with a glass exists for exactly that failure mode.

title: Hang the scoop on its own hook
instruction: The scoop goes back on its dedicated hook outside the well, not left sitting in the ice.
rationale: A scoop left buried in the ice gets grabbed by the handle end covered in melt and hands, which defeats the entire point of using a scoop instead of a glass — the hook keeps it out of the ice and off the bar top between uses, where it stays a clean tool instead of another surface the ice sits against.

title: Glove up before touching the garnish
instruction: Gloves on before the citrus or the tray.
rationale: Ready-to-eat garnish that goes straight into a drink with no cooking step in between is exactly the category the Retail Food Code's bare-hand-contact rule covers — gloves go on before the knife, not after the first wedge is already cut.

title: Cut, fill and date the garnish
instruction: Cut the citrus, fill the tray inserts, then label the tray with today's date — in that order.
rationale: A garnish tray dated at the start of shift is how anyone opening tomorrow's shift knows whether what's left is still good, and cutting before filling before dating is the only order that does not mean re-touching product after it is already labelled done.

title: Check the glass washer's temperature and chemical
instruction: Run a cycle and read the final rinse gauge — commit once it lands in the sanitising band.
rationale: The Retail Food Code sets the standard a glass washer's sanitising rinse has to hit, by heat or by chemical, and an NSF-listed machine only meets that standard while it's actually running to spec — checking it cold at the start of shift is the only way to know every glass tonight is coming out sanitised rather than just rinsed and shiny.

title: Pour-test the well bottles
instruction: Hold a steady, counted speed-pour into the test jigger — too fast overpours, too slow underpours.
rationale: Every well bottle gets a new speed pourer at the start of shift, and a pourer poured too fast or too slow all night is either giving product away or shorting every drink built from it — pour-testing against the jigger before service is how the whole bar's cost and consistency get set at once instead of drink by drink.

title: Count the till float
instruction: Count the opening drawer against the float sheet before the first sale.
rationale: California Labor Code §351 makes clear that whatever is in a tip jar belongs to the staff who earned it, and a float counted and signed for before service is the same discipline applied to the house's own money — an uncounted drawer is a dispute waiting to happen the first time it comes up short at close.

title: Walk the bar before the doors open
instruction: One more pass along the whole line before the first guest — click anything left wrong.
rationale: Every step so far was checked once, in isolation; the walk is where a bartender looks at the bar the way a guest is about to see it, and it is the last chance to catch the one thing that got missed between two otherwise-clean checks.

situation: The barback is reaching for a rocks glass off the rail to scoop the fresh ice into the well.
instruction: Stop them — hand them the scoop.
missed: The barback scooped the new ice with the glass anyway. A chip off that glass is now somewhere in the well, and there is no way to find it again once it's mixed into a full bin of ice.

situation: A customer who came in early is leaning over the bar, reaching for the open garnish tray while you're mid pour-test.
instruction: Glove up and take control of the tray before they touch it bare-handed.
missed: The customer got a hand into the tray before anyone stopped them. Every wedge in that tray is now a bare-hand-contact question, and the only honest fix left is to toss the tray and cut a fresh one.

explanation: The till drawer is sitting open with nobody at it. An unattended open drawer during setup is a loss-prevention problem before the shift has even started, and it is the float count itself — done once, counted, and closed — that is supposed to be the only time it is open before service.

You left a phone propped against the till showing the cocktail menu instead of using the printed one behind the bar. A phone screen face-down in a wet well is a cracked screen and a distraction during a headcount, not a menu — the printed one lives back here for exactly that reason.

That spray bottle has sanitiser in it with no label on it. Cal/OSHA hazard communication under 8 CCR §5194, built on the same federal OSHA standard at 29 CFR 1910.1200, requires a secondary container to say what is actually inside it — the next person to reach for it, mid-rush, is trusting a bottle that could be anything.

Ice melt is pooling by the well with no wet-floor sign out. A bar floor is wet by the nature of the job; the sign is what turns a normal shift hazard into a marked one, and Cal/OSHA's Injury and Illness Prevention Program under 8 CCR §3203 expects exactly this kind of routine hazard controlled before it is stepped in.

title: Check today's menu against the meal pattern
instruction: Read the posted menu and confirm all five meal-pattern components are on the line.
rationale: A reimbursable lunch needs a meat/meat alternate, a grain, a fruit, a vegetable and milk on the line every day — not on every tray, on the line — because a student who is only offered four of the five cannot build a reimbursable meal no matter what they choose. The board is the line's own check against the federal count before a single tray moves.

title: Fill the steam table's water bath
instruction: Open the fill valve until the water bath under the wells is at its working level.
rationale: A steam table heats through the water bath, not directly on the pan, and a well run dry heats its own empty tank instead of the food sitting in it — that is exactly how an element burns out mid-service. Filling it before service starts is the whole difference between a well that holds temperature for four hours and one that fails on the busiest line of the day.

title: Probe the hot well
instruction: Probe the entrée pan and commit once the well reads 135°F or above.
rationale: The well's own thermostat tells you where it is set, not what the food in the pan actually is — a full pan loaded cold can sit under temperature for the first twenty minutes even with the element running correctly. The probe in the food is the number that actually decides whether the line can open.

title: Probe the cold pan
instruction: Probe the fruit cups in the cold well and commit once it reads 41°F or below.
rationale: Cold holding runs the same rule in the other direction: 41°F or below, checked in the food itself rather than assumed from the unit's dial. Fruit and salad items sit in the danger zone just as fast climbing up from 41°F as a hot item does falling from 135°F — the well only protects a tray that is actually probed.

title: Check the milk cooler
instruction: Read the milk cooler's thermometer and confirm it holds at 41°F or below.
rationale: Milk is the one component on every tray that never gets probed individually — the whole case lives or dies on whether the cooler itself is holding, which is why the cooler's own thermometer is checked before the first carton comes out, not discovered cold or warm one carton at a time.

title: Wash hands before gloving up
instruction: Hold at the hand sink and scrub before pulling on gloves for the ready-to-eat station.
rationale: Gloves go over clean hands, not instead of them — a glove pulled onto unwashed hands just moves whatever was on the skin onto the inside of the glove, where the next contact spreads it straight back out. The wash happens first, every time gloves come off and go back on.

title: Walk the line before the bell
instruction: Three things on this line are not right. Find them before the first tray comes through.
rationale: The line is walked with your own eyes before service the same way a buffet is — a portion tool, a guard panel and a glove box are all things a server has to trust are correct all shift, and the only point anybody actually checks them is right now, before the first student is standing in front of the pan.

title: Check the dietary cards at the register
instruction: Confirm today's allergy and dietary accommodation cards are current at the point of service.
rationale: A medically documented food allergy gets a substitution under the meal pattern's own rule, and the register is the only point in the whole line where a name on a tray meets a name on a card — miss it here and there is no second checkpoint before the tray reaches the table.

title: Serve a full reimbursable tray
instruction: Serve all five components in the order the line is set up: entrée, grain, vegetable, fruit, milk.
rationale: Offer versus serve only works if all five components are actually offered at every tray — the student chooses at least three, one of which has to be a fruit or a vegetable, but that choice is theirs to make only if a server put all five in front of them first. Skipping one at the pan is a choice the server made for them.

title: Hold the line's pace
instruction: Keep the serving rate in the band that matches the lunch period without rushing the portions.
rationale: A twenty-five-minute lunch period is the actual clock this line runs on — serve too slowly and half the students eat in the last five minutes of their own lunch; rush it and portion sizes are the first thing that slips, which quietly turns a reimbursable meal into one that no longer meets the pattern.

title: Send the tray to the register
instruction: Carry the completed tray to the register for the reimbursable count.
rationale: The register is where the meal actually gets counted for reimbursement, and it only counts a tray it can see was served — a tray that skips the register because the line is backed up is food served for free that the program never gets credit for feeding.

title: Reconcile the day's count
instruction: Match the register total against the tray count at the end of service.
rationale: The claim the cafeteria files is only as good as the number behind it, and the two counts — trays served and register rings — are supposed to match. A gap between them is either a tray that walked past the register or a number somebody is going to have to explain to the district.

title: Close the production record
instruction: Log the temperatures taken, the portions served and the components offered on the day's production record.
rationale: The production record is the paperwork that proves the meal pattern was actually met on a given day, not just planned — it is what a state auditor reads first, and it is also the only place tonight's temperatures survive past the end of the shift that took them.

situation: A student with a milk allergy card on file is at the register, and there's a carton of milk sitting on their tray.
instruction: That card means a substitution, not a carton.
missed: The tray went through with the milk still on it. A documented allergy caught after the student has already left the line is a phone call home, not a substitution.

situation: The hot well's heating element has just dropped out — the entrée pan is losing temperature and the line behind it is backing up.
instruction: Nothing serves from a well that isn't holding. Find the fix, not the ladle.
missed: Service kept moving off a well that had already failed. Every tray served from it after that point was served from food nobody can say was still 135°F or above.

explanation: That is a bare hand going into the fruit cups. Ready-to-eat food gets no further kill step before a student eats it, so a bare hand is the last thing that touches it before they do — gloves or tongs, every time, on anything already ready to serve.

Those gloves went from making change at the register straight back onto the line. Cash is one of the dirtiest things that crosses this counter all day, and a glove that touched it and then touched food has carried that contact onto every tray after it.

That pan has tree nuts in it and there is no allergen card posted at the station. A line worker who does not know an item contains a top allergen cannot answer the one question a parent or a student is most likely to ask.

That crate has been sitting on the counter, not in the cooler. Milk out of refrigeration is climbing out of the temperature the Food Code and the milk cooler are both built around, and a warm carton on a tray is one a parent complains about before it is ever a safety problem.

title: Check the tab before you check him
instruction: Open his tab on the till: drink count and how long he has been running it.
rationale: The count and the clock are the two facts an RBS decision is actually built on — a fourth drink in forty minutes reads completely differently from a fourth drink in three hours, and the till is the only thing in the room keeping an honest number.

title: Read the four RBS cues before you pour again
instruction: Speech, coordination, judgement, appearance — look for all four before the next drink goes out.
rationale: The RBS curriculum teaches exactly these four categories because any one of them alone can have an innocent explanation, and two or more together are what actually separates a customer who has had a long week from one who is obviously intoxicated under §25602.

title: Slow him down with water before you slow him down with a decision
instruction: Set a water glass down without being asked.
rationale: Slowing service starts before the cutoff conversation does. A water glass costs nothing, buys time for the cues to either resolve or confirm themselves, and never has to be explained to anybody.

title: Offer food off the kitchen's menu
instruction: Slide the food menu across — something in front of him slows the pace on its own.
rationale: Food in the stomach does nothing to reverse intoxication that has already happened, but it slows the rate a customer keeps drinking at, and it gives you a second reasonable thing to be doing besides watching the clock on his tab.

title: If one more round is coming, make it a smaller one
instruction: Pour to the reduced line on the metered spout, not the standard one.
rationale: A reduced pour is a real intervention, not a compromise — it buys the table another twenty minutes to sober up on the same tab, and it is the difference between a bar that slowed service and a bar that just kept serving more slowly.

title: Swap the free-pour spout for the metered one
instruction: Turn the collar until the metered pourer seats — no more free pours to this table tonight.
rationale: A metered spout takes the judgement call out of the bottle itself: it cannot be talked into a heavier pour by a customer who has already lost the judgement to ask for one fairly.

title: Keep your eyes on the table while the decision forms
instruction: Hold your attention on him and the table around him for a moment before you commit to the cutoff.
rationale: The decision to cut somebody off is made by watching, not by a single glance — RBS training is explicit that the cues are confirmed over a minute or two, not diagnosed on the first pass across the room.

title: Have the conversation quietly and without arguing
instruction: Approach him alone and low-key, say the decision plainly once, then offer the alternative.
rationale: The order matters: a quiet approach before the words keeps the table from feeling ambushed, naming it plainly once removes any room to negotiate it away, and the offer that follows is what turns a refusal into a decision he can leave with instead of a fight he has to win.

title: Flag the tab in the till
instruction: Mark his tab so the register itself refuses the next round.
rationale: A flag on the tab is the difference between a decision that lives in your head for the next ten minutes and one that survives you getting busy at the other end of the bar.

title: Tell the rest of the shift by name
instruction: Call it out to whoever else is working the floor — not just the till.
rationale: The POS flag stops one register. A cutoff that only exists on a screen does not stop a barback covering your section for five minutes, or a server who never looked at the tab, from pouring him one anyway.

title: Stay with it after the words are said
instruction: Keep watching the table and the door while you finish the rest of the shift's business.
rationale: A cutoff is not finished when the sentence is finished. The two minutes after it — before the ride is actually arranged — are when a table gets a second drink from a friend or a customer who has decided he does not need one.

title: Take the keys off the bar and lock them up
instruction: Move his keys from the bar top into the lockbox — nobody drives on them tonight.
rationale: Dram-shop liability does not end at the sale — it follows the guest out the door. Physically taking the keys off the bar is worth more than any conversation about whether he is fine to drive.

title: Arrange the ride before he leaves the stool
instruction: Call a rideshare, a cab, or the friend who is actually sober.
rationale: An offer to call a ride that is never followed through is not a safe cutoff, it is a sentence said to make the conversation feel finished — the ride has to actually be on its way before anyone stands up.

title: Write the cutoff into the log
instruction: Log the time, the drink count, the cues you saw, and how he got home.
rationale: A written cutoff — time, count, cues, outcome — is what the licence and your own name are protected by if tonight is ever the night that gets asked about later. An unlogged cutoff is a story two people remember differently.

situation: His friend has just ordered two beers off the tap list and is sliding one straight across the table to him.
instruction: The cutoff has not even started and the table is already covering for him.
missed: The glass stayed in front of him and he drank from it. Every RBS cue you were watching for is still true, and the table just proved a cutoff has to cover the friend as well as the register.

situation: He has stood up off the stool, picked his keys up off the bar, and is walking toward the door and the car park.
instruction: The ride is not called yet and he already has his keys out.
missed: He walked out with his own keys in his hand. Everything from the cues to the quiet cutoff protected the bar's licence for exactly as long as it took him to reach the car park — dram-shop liability does not stop at the door.

explanation: That bottle has no metered pourer on it. A free pour to a guest already showing every RBS cue is exactly the sale §25602 exists to stop, and it is also the sale a dram-shop claim is built out of afterward — the reduced, measured pour is not a suggestion, it is the whole legal difference.
The relief board is still blank. The POS flag stops the register; it does not stop the next bartender who never heard about this table from pouring him one anyway the moment your shift ends.

You said it into the room instead of to him. A cutoff announced over the bar mic or across three feet of open air turns a quiet decision into a public one, and a customer who has just been embarrassed in front of his table is a customer who argues instead of leaving.

That is the quick-key that rings another round to his tab. A flag on the till only works if nobody presses through it — one more pour after the cutoff undoes the whole conversation and puts the sale back on the same obviously-intoxicated customer §25602 was written for.

title: Read the SDS for the dish machine chemicals
instruction: Open the binder and check the sanitiser and detergent sheets before the shift starts.
rationale: The safety data sheet is where the incompatibility warning actually lives — OSHA's hazard communication standard puts it on the shelf specifically so nobody has to guess which chemicals can and cannot share a line, a bucket or a spill.

title: Check the dispenser's concentrate lines
instruction: Trace both concentrate lines from their jugs to the dispenser before trusting either one.
rationale: The dispenser cabinet is the one place in the pit where the chemicals are still full strength and where two lines running an inch apart are simple to cross by mistake. A line checked here is the difference between the machine actually working and a proportioner confidently metering the wrong chemical all shift.

title: Glove and apron up for the chemicals
instruction: Pull on the chemical-resistant gloves and the rubber apron before touching the dispenser or the sink.
rationale: Everything at this station — concentrate, sanitiser solution, hot rinse water — is something dish soap and a t-shirt were never rated for. The gloves and apron are staged here rather than at the line because this is the one job in the kitchen where a splash is concentrated rather than diluted.

title: Read the dish machine's final-rinse gauge
instruction: Watch the final-rinse temperature climb through a cycle and commit once it holds in the Food Code's range for a high-temperature machine.
rationale: A high-temperature machine sanitises with heat instead of chemical, and the Food Code's final-rinse number is the only proof that happened — a machine that sounds right and smells like hot water can still be running a rinse ten degrees short, which is a load of dishes that only ever got washed.

title: Set up the three-compartment sink
instruction: Fill wash, then rinse, then sanitise — in that order, left to right.
rationale: Each compartment undoes what the last one left behind: wash lifts the soil, rinse clears the detergent, sanitise is the last thing touching the item before it drains dry. Filled out of order, detergent or food soil ends up carried into the sanitiser and neutralises it before the first item ever goes in.

title: Test the sanitiser with a strip
instruction: Dip the strip in the sanitise compartment, read it against the colour chart, and commit the concentration.
rationale: A dispenser set correctly and a dispenser actually delivering that setting are two different claims, and the strip is the only one of them that is measured rather than assumed. Chlorine sanitiser has to land in the 50 to 100 ppm band — a quaternary sanitiser is read against its own label — and nothing on the machine's dial can substitute for that colour change.

title: Log the sanitiser reading
instruction: Write the ppm reading and the time on the concentration log before the first rack goes in.
rationale: A verified reading nobody wrote down is a fact only for as long as it stays in your head. The log is what turns this shift's test into something a health inspector, the next shift or a steward can actually check without redoing the test themselves.

title: Hold the sanitise contact time
instruction: Submerge the item in the sanitise compartment and hold it for the full contact time the concentration and water temperature call for.
rationale: Sanitiser kills on a curve, not on contact — pull an item the instant it touches the solution and it has been wetted, not sanitised. The Food Code's contact time exists because that curve needs seconds to finish, and a rushed dip is a load that looks identical to a properly sanitised one until somebody gets sick.

title: Prove the eyewash runs clear
instruction: Push the paddle valve and hold it open until the flow runs clear of any standing water or rust.
rationale: ANSI/ISEA Z358.1 calls for a weekly activation test for exactly this reason: the header pipe on an eyewash sits full of stagnant water between uses, and a station nobody has tested delivers a faceful of rust and bacteria to somebody who is already having the worst minute of their shift.

title: Drill the fifteen-minute flush
instruction: Hold your own eyes in the stream and don't stop early — a real splash gets the full flush, not a quick rinse.
rationale: ANSI/ISEA Z358.1 calls for a continuous fifteen-minute flush for a chemical splash to the eye, timed from the moment the water starts, because a sanitiser or delimer concentrate keeps reacting with tissue for as long as any of it is still on the surface — stopping at the two-minute mark most people's instinct hits leaves the reaction still running.

title: Take the SDS to the clinic
instruction: Pull the copy of the sanitiser's SDS off the binder to send with the injured worker.
rationale: Whoever treats a chemical exposure needs to know exactly what was in the eye, not a guess at the brand name — the SDS is what tells a clinic or an ER the pH, the concentration and the first-aid measures the manufacturer actually tested, in the time it takes to hand over a sheet of paper.

title: Stage the clean rack on the cart
instruction: Carry the stacked rack to the rolling cart rather than across the floor by hand.
rationale: A stacked rack carried at arm's length blocks the one hand that would otherwise catch a slip, on the one floor in the kitchen that is reliably wet. The cart carries the weight and the height instead of your wrists and your sightline.

title: Walk the pit before you leave it
instruction: Check the floor and the chemical shelf before handing the station to the next shift.
rationale: The pit is about to run unattended between shifts or during a break, and a puddle or an open jug does not wait politely for somebody to notice — the walk-through is the last chance to catch either one before it becomes the next person's surprise.

situation: The strip you just dipped mid-shift comes back with no colour change at all — the dispenser is pulling nothing but water.
instruction: The sanitiser jug behind the dispenser is empty. Swap it before another rack goes through that compartment.
missed: Racks kept moving through a sanitise compartment that had stopped sanitising an unknown number of cycles ago, and nothing on the floor caught it because nobody looked at the jug.

situation: The prep cook refilling the delimer bottle at the dispenser just took a faceful off the spout and is calling out — eyes shut, hands over her face.
instruction: Get her onto the second eyewash head now — don't wait for her to find it herself.
missed: She stood there with her eyes shut for the whole window instead of being walked to the second head, and every second of that is chlorine sitting on the cornea instead of being flushed off it.

explanation: You stacked that rack higher than your own sightline and carried it at arm's length across a wet floor instead of loading it on the cart. A dropped stack on quarry tile is a laceration and a burn in the same fall; the cart exists so nobody's hands are the thing balancing a hundred pounds of hot glassware over a slick floor.

You reached into the concentrate jug with a bare hand. Warewashing chemicals are the reason gloves and an apron are staged at this station specifically, not a general kitchen rule — a splash off a jug lip is concentrate, not the diluted solution in the sink.

Somebody parked the mop bucket in front of the eyewash. ANSI/ISEA Z358.1 calls for that station to be reachable in about ten seconds with nothing in the way, because a person flushing a chemical splash cannot see well enough to step around a bucket first.

That concentrate line is plumbed into the wrong inlet on the dispenser — the chlorine sanitiser and an acid-based delimer sharing one draw line. The SDS for both is explicit about this: chlorine plus an acid gives off chlorine gas, and it does that inside a closed dispenser cabinet a foot from where somebody is standing.

title: Identify the cleaner and its SDS
instruction: Check the drum label, then pull the matching safety data sheet.
rationale: A bar alternates between caustic and acid line cleaners depending on what's building up in the lines, and the two are handled differently enough — different PPE, different first aid, never mixed with each other — that the whole clean starts with confirming which one is actually in the bucket today.

title: Goggles and gloves before the bottle opens
instruction: Both on before the cleaner comes off the shelf.
rationale: Caustic and acid line cleaners are both corrosive to skin and eyes at working strength, and a splash happens at the moment you're least braced for it — opening the container, not partway through pumping — which is why the PPE goes on first, not after the first splash proves it was needed.

title: Stage the spill kit
instruction: Set the spill kit where you can reach it before you start pumping.
rationale: A corrosive spill on a bar top full of glassware and electrical outlets is not something you want to be locating supplies for after it happens — staging the kit first is what makes the response take ten seconds instead of two minutes.

title: Tag every affected tap "Do Not Pour"
instruction: Tag all three handles on this line before any cleaner goes in.
rationale: A customer at the rail and a colleague working the well both read a tap handle the same way — available unless it says otherwise. Every handle on the line being cleaned gets its own tag, because the one left untagged is the one somebody pours from.

title: Disconnect the keg for the cleaning loop
instruction: Uncouple the keg and swap the line onto the cleaning pump.
rationale: Cleaning solution runs a closed loop through the line and back to the bucket, not into a keg of beer — the coupler comes off and the pump goes on before any solution moves.

title: Pump the cleaning solution through
instruction: Hold the pump running until solution has moved all the way through the line.
rationale: A partial pump leaves clean beer in one stretch of tubing and cleaner in the next, and neither half gets what it needs — the whole line has to see the solution before contact time means anything.

title: Hold contact time
instruction: Let the solution sit in the line for the full contact time on the label.
rationale: The chemical does its work by sitting against the beer-stone and yeast film built up on the inside of the tubing, not by passing through it — cutting the contact time short is the single most common reason a line that was 'just cleaned' still tastes off a week later.

title: Flush the line with water
instruction: Hold the flush valve at a steady rate until the line runs clear.
rationale: Too slow a flush leaves cleaner sitting in the low points of the line; too hard a flush can push water back past a fitting that isn't rated for it — a steady, held-open flow is what actually clears the tubing end to end.

title: Test the line with pH paper
instruction: Dip the strip at the tap and commit while it reads neutral.
rationale: A line that still reads acidic or basic still has cleaning chemical in it no matter how much water has gone through — the strip is the only honest answer to 'is it out yet,' and neutral is the only reading that means yes.

title: Reconnect the kegs
instruction: Couple the keg back onto the now-neutral line.
rationale: The line only goes back into beer service once the pH test has confirmed there's nothing left in it to confirm against — reconnecting on a hunch instead of a reading is exactly the shortcut this whole procedure exists to remove.

title: Discard the first pour and clear the tags
instruction: Pour and dump the first glass off each tap, then pull the "Do Not Pour" tags.
rationale: The first pour off a freshly cleaned line still carries trace cleaner and the standing water from the flush — it gets poured out, not into a glass someone's paying for, and the tags come off only once there's a clean pour behind them to prove it.

title: Log the clean
instruction: Record the date, the chemical, the contact time and the final pH.
rationale: The cleaning log is what turns 'we did this' into something a health inspector, the next shift or the brewery's own quality rep can actually check against a schedule instead of taking on faith.

situation: A customer orders an IPA off the tagged tap, and a colleague reaches for the handle to pour it.
instruction: Stop them — that handle's tagged for a reason, not out of service by accident.
missed: The colleague poured off the tagged IPA tap while it was still running cleaning solution. A tag that gets overridden the first time someone's in a hurry isn't protecting anybody.

situation: The open cleaner bottle gets knocked over on the bar top behind you.
instruction: Get to the spill kit — don't just wipe it with a bar rag.
missed: The spill got wiped up with a bar rag instead of the spill kit. Spreading a corrosive thinner across the bar top, and onto the rag itself, is worse than the spill it started as.

explanation: You leaned in over the open cleaner to look — no goggles. A splash off a moving line or a bucket doesn't wait for you to notice it's coming, and the label on a caustic or acid line cleaner says eye protection for exactly this reason, not as a formality before the real work starts.

That's an acid-based cleaner sitting open next to the caustic bucket already in use. Acid and caustic line cleaners meeting each other, whether in a drain or a bucket, react hard enough to throw a corrosive splash and a cloud of gas — the SDS for each one exists specifically so they never share a container or a moment.

The line cleaner's been decanted into a spray bottle with no label on it. Cal/OSHA's hazard communication rule follows the chemical, not the original container — an unlabeled bottle of caustic under the bar is a bottle nobody after you will know to treat with any caution at all.

This tap handle never got tagged with the others. A line mid-clean that isn't tagged looks exactly like a line that's ready to pour, and the only thing standing between a customer and a glass of line cleaner is whether every handle got marked, not just most of them.

title: Read today's delivery manifest
instruction: Read the manifest for what's arriving and what temperature each item should hold.
rationale: The manifest is what tells the receiving worker whether a pallet of frozen goods is actually supposed to be frozen solid or partly thawed by design — without reading it first, a temperature reading at the dock means nothing to compare it against.

title: Probe the delivery truck's temperature
instruction: Probe a case from the reefer and commit the reading against the manifest's expected range.
rationale: A reefer unit's own dial says where the truck's controls are set, not what the product inside actually reached over the whole trip — probing the food itself is the only way to know it never left the safe range between the supplier's dock and this one.

title: Inspect the delivery before it comes off the dock
instruction: Three things about this delivery are not right. Find them before it comes inside.
rationale: The dock is the one point in the whole chain where a bad case can be turned around and sent back rather than becoming this kitchen's problem — every one of these three signs is easy to miss once the pallet is already broken down and shelved among cases that are fine.

title: Set the damaged case aside for return
instruction: Carry the case with the swollen can to the return pallet, separate from accepted stock.
rationale: A rejected case has to physically leave the path to the shelves, not just get a note written about it — the return pallet is where it goes so nobody restocking later mistakes it for something already cleared.

title: Date and rotate the stock
instruction: Date-label the new delivery, move the oldest stock to the front, then place the new stock behind it, in that order.
rationale: First-in-first-out only works if the oldest stock is actually in front of the newest, and it stays that way only if new stock always goes in behind — dating comes first because a shelf full of undated cases has no way to know which one is oldest at all.

title: Dial in the sanitizer dispenser
instruction: Turn the dispenser's selector to the sanitizer's labelled concentration.
rationale: The dispenser is built to hit one specific concentration reliably, the same way the dilution station in the supply closet is — turning the selector to the label's own setting is what makes the test strip step that follows a confirmation instead of a guess.

title: Test the sanitizer concentration
instruction: Dip the test strip and commit the reading against the label's required band.
rationale: The dispenser's dial says where it's set, not what actually came out of it today — the test strip is the only proof the basin or the machine is actually sanitizing at the concentration the label calls for, checked fresh at the start of the shift.

title: Hold dishes through the sanitizer's contact time
instruction: Hold the basket submerged for the full contact time before pulling it out.
rationale: A dish pulled early has been in the sanitizer without actually reaching the exposure time the label's concentration is built around — the basket stays down for the whole hold, not until it looks clean, because looking clean and being sanitized are two different things.

title: Feed the dish machine at a steady rate
instruction: Keep the rack feed rate steady as the machine runs.
rationale: A rack fed too fast doesn't give the machine's own wash-rinse-sanitize cycle time to finish on each load, and one fed too slow backs up everything behind it — a steady feed rate is what keeps every rack getting the full cycle it needs.

title: Move the clean rack to storage
instruction: Carry the finished rack of clean dishes to the drying and storage shelf.
rationale: A clean rack left sitting at the machine's outfeed is a clean rack at risk of getting splashed by the next dirty load coming through — moving it straight to storage keeps sanitized dishes sanitized until they're actually needed.

title: Log receiving temps and sanitizer readings
instruction: Record the delivery temperature, the rejected case and today's sanitizer concentration.
rationale: The log is the kitchen's own proof, if a health inspector or the district ever asks, that the delivery was actually checked and the sanitizer actually tested today — a clean dish room with no record behind it can't answer that question.

title: Close down the kitchen
instruction: Cover the floor drains, lock the chemicals away, then turn off the lights, in that order.
rationale: Chemicals get locked away before the lights go off because that's the one closing task that keeps food and cleaning chemicals apart overnight — the drains and the lights matter, but a chemical cabinet left unlocked overnight is the one mistake that's still a problem when the doors open again tomorrow.

situation: A server has grabbed a stack of plates straight off the rack, before the sanitizer's contact time actually finished.
instruction: Ring the pass-through bell and call them back now.
missed: The plates left the dish room before contact time finished — sanitizer at the right concentration still needs its full time to work, and a shortened dip is the same as skipping it.

situation: A stack of trays has jammed sideways in the dish machine, and the belt is grinding against them.
instruction: Hit the emergency stop.
missed: The belt kept grinding against the jam — a machine that stays powered while jammed is one more turn away from damaging the belt or catching a hand reaching in to clear it.
