explanation: That can is swollen at both ends and it's headed for the shelf anyway. A swollen can is a sign of gas from bacterial growth inside it, and it gets rejected on sight — not opened, not tasted, not shelved next to cans that are fine.

That's a bare hand going into the hot sanitizer basin instead of the tongs or the rack. The basin runs hot enough to scald and concentrated enough to irritate skin on prolonged contact — hands stay out of it, full stop.

That's a shelf of cleaning chemicals sitting directly above open food product. Anything that leaks or gets knocked off that shelf lands in the food below it — chemicals are stored below and away from food, never over it.

That's mixing the sanitizer by eye instead of reading the test strip. A solution too weak doesn't actually sanitize anything sitting in it for the full contact time, and one too strong is its own hazard on food-contact surfaces — the strip is what turns a guess into a known concentration.

title: Read the service ticket
instruction: Confirm which fryer, which oil grade, and which boil-out chemical the ticket calls for.
rationale: Two fryers on the same line can run different oils and different boil-out chemicals, and the ticket is what tells you which is which — working from memory on a busy line is how the wrong chemical ends up soaking a stainless vat it was never rated for.

title: Shut the fryer off
instruction: Kill the fryer at its power switch before anything else moves.
rationale: Nothing about this job — not the drain, not the caddy, not the boil-out — happens with the fryer still calling for heat. Shutting it off first is what makes every reading you take after this point actually mean something, instead of chasing a temperature the burner is still adding to.

title: Confirm the oil has cooled
instruction: Watch the vat thermometer and commit once it reads inside the plan's safe-to-drain band.
rationale: Fryer oil at cooking temperature is close to 350°F, and oil at that heat splashes through a sleeve and blisters skin on contact — the plan's cool-down band exists because the drain valve and the caddy are both rated for a specific temperature ceiling, not for whatever the vat happens to read when somebody feels like starting.

title: Don the burn PPE
instruction: Apron, then sleeve guards, then face shield, then the thermal gloves last.
rationale: The gloves go on last because everything before them needs bare fingers to fasten straps and buckles, and putting them on first just means peeling them off again for the apron ties. Every piece is on before the drain valve is touched — a splash you did not expect is the whole reason this order exists.

title: Roll the oil caddy into place
instruction: Position the wheeled caddy directly under the drain, not a bucket.
rationale: The caddy is a sealed, wheeled tank sized for exactly this vat, and it is the only container this drain ever runs into. A bucket set under the same valve holds the same oil at the same temperature with none of the caddy's lid, wheels or capacity margin.

title: Open the drain valve
instruction: Turn the drain valve handle to fully open and let the vat empty into the caddy.
rationale: A drain valve stopped part way still passes oil, just slower and less predictably, and a slow stream is exactly what lets it wander off the caddy's inlet. Take the handle all the way to its stop so the flow is a straight line into the tank you positioned for it.

title: Hold the caddy under the flow
instruction: Stay at the caddy while the vat empties completely — do not walk away mid-drain.
rationale: Oil coming off a full vat does not run at a constant rate — it surges as pockets of sediment and breading debris clear the strainer, and a caddy left unattended under a surging drain is how oil ends up on the floor around it instead of inside the tank. Staying at the caddy is what catches that the moment it happens.

title: Find the correct boil-out chemical
instruction: Three bottles are on the shelf. Take the one the ticket actually called for.
rationale: A boil-out chemical is matched to the vat's metal and to the specific baked-on residue it is meant to lift, and the shelf next to it holds two other chemicals that are wrong for entirely different reasons — reading the label against the ticket is the only step between the right bottle and a ruined vat.

title: Boil out the vat
instruction: Work the brush over the vat walls and hold through the chemical's full contact time.
rationale: A boil-out only lifts carbonized oil off the vat wall if the chemical stays in contact long enough to do its job, and pulling the brush away early just spreads a half-dissolved film around instead of removing it — the vat gets scrubbed for the full time the label calls for, not until it looks close enough.

title: Wheel the caddy to the rendering bin
instruction: Roll the caddy along the dry route to the rendering bin — do not cross the anti-fatigue mats.
rationale: A loaded caddy rolling over the seam of a raised anti-fatigue mat can catch a wheel and tip, which is exactly the failure this whole procedure has been built to avoid since the vat was drained — the dry route around the mats exists because used oil at rest is still hot enough to matter for a good while after it leaves the vat.

title: Fill fresh oil to the line
instruction: Pour the fresh oil and commit once the level sits at the fill mark.
rationale: The fill line is not a suggestion — the manufacturer set it to the volume that keeps oil circulating past the heating element instead of scorching against it, and it is also the margin that keeps a lowered basket from displacing oil over the rim onto a hot cabinet.

title: Confirm the element is covered
instruction: Check that the fresh oil fully covers the heating element before power goes back on.
rationale: An element sitting above the oil line dry-fires the instant it is energized, and it does that in seconds, not minutes — NSF-listed fryers put the fill mark exactly at the depth the element needs, and confirming the cover before the switch is touched is what keeps that mark meaningful.

title: Power the fryer back on
instruction: Return the fryer to service now that the element is covered and the vat is filled.
rationale: This is the one point in the whole job where the fryer is allowed to call for heat again, and it is allowed only because every step ahead of it — cooldown, drain, boil-out, refill, covered element — is already done. Reaching the switch any earlier turns one of those into an assumption instead of a confirmed fact.

title: Mop the floor around the fryer dry
instruction: Sweep the mop steadily across the marked area until it reads dry.
rationale: Every step before this one put oil, boil-out runoff or rinse water on this floor at some point, and none of it counts as finished until the tile is actually dry under foot — a fry cook, a food runner or the closer doing inventory is the next person to stand exactly here.

situation: The caddy's drain hose has kicked loose off the fitting. Oil is running down the front of the tank onto the floor instead of into it.
instruction: Secure the hose before that stream reaches the walkway.
missed: The hose stayed loose and oil kept running down the caddy onto the tile. That puddle sits directly on the route the caddy itself is about to be wheeled over, and it is still close to hot.

situation: A co-worker has walked up to the fryer's power switch, thinking the boil-out is finished, with the element still sitting bare inside an empty vat.
instruction: Stop that switch before the bare element gets power.
missed: The switch got flipped with the element bare in an empty vat. A dry-fired element heats unopposed by any oil to carry the heat away, and it fails — or ignites whatever film is left in the vat — inside seconds.

explanation: That is a mop bucket, not the wheeled oil caddy. Oil off this drain is still within a few degrees of scalding when the plan calls it safe to move, and a bucket has no lid, no wheel and nothing stopping it tipping the moment a boot catches its rim — the caddy is a sealed, wheeled tank built to take that heat between the fryer and the rendering bin, and it is the only container this job uses.

That bucket is full and somebody is about to carry it by hand across the line. Hot oil in an open container held at arm's length has no lid holding it level and no wheels absorbing a stumble, and a spill from carrying height lands on feet, not floor. Cal/OSHA's walking-working-surface rules exist for exactly this kind of load — wheel it, never carry it.

The heating element is still bare — no oil covering it and no guard over it. Energizing a fryer element with nothing over it dry-fires the coil toward burnout in seconds and, with any residual oil vapor still in the vat, gives that vapor an ignition source it would not otherwise have. The element gets covered by fresh oil before the switch is touched, not after.

That slick by the fryer is still wet. Quarry tile with a film of fryer oil on it has close to the grip of wet ice, and the next person through here is carrying either hot oil or a full basket. The floor gets dried before the station is called finished, not left for whoever crosses it next to discover.

title: Read the alarm annunciator
instruction: Check the annunciator panel to see which zone tripped the ammonia alarm.
rationale: The panel is the first fact this whole response runs on — which zone tripped tells the plan's own muster and headcount who was actually in the affected area, and it's read once, on the way out, not investigated up close.

title: Commit to evacuate, not investigate
instruction: Confirm the call: leave the machine room now, per the plant's own emergency plan.
rationale: The plan does not ask an engineer to confirm the leak by smell, by sound or by looking for it — it asks for an immediate evacuation the moment the alarm sounds, because the alternative is one person's judgment standing in for a plan built by people who were not standing in the room when it went off.

title: Close the machine room door behind you
instruction: Pull the door shut behind you as you leave, rather than leaving it open.
rationale: A door pulled shut behind you is the plant's own first layer of containment — it keeps whatever is in that room in that room for the minutes it takes a responder to actually arrive.

title: Notice two things on your way out
instruction: Two things along your evacuation route are worth reporting. Find them without stopping.
rationale: Evacuating is not the same as evacuating with your eyes closed — noticing what's wrong on the way out, without stopping to fix any of it, is what gives the responders arriving behind you a fuller picture than the alarm alone gives them.

title: Check the wind indicator before mustering
instruction: Read the wind sock and commit once your route to muster is upwind of the plant.
rationale: Ammonia is lighter than air and disperses with the wind, so the muster point the plan posted only does its job if you actually approach it from upwind — the sock is what confirms that before you commit to a route, not after you're already standing in the wrong spot.

title: Move to the muster point on the marked route
instruction: Walk briskly on the marked route — not a run, not a stroll — the whole way to muster.
rationale: A run risks a fall on a route other people are also using; a stroll leaves you and everyone behind you closer to the affected zone longer than the plan intends. A steady, brisk pace on the marked route is what the plan is actually asking for.

title: Check in at the muster roster
instruction: Mark yourself present on the muster point's roster board.
rationale: A muster point only proves everyone is out once every name on the shift roster is actually accounted for — the board is what turns "I think everyone made it" into a fact somebody can act on.

title: Hold your position at muster
instruction: Stay at the muster point and hold until authorized personnel give the all-clear.
rationale: The muster point does its job only if people actually stay there — drifting off to check on the building, your car or anything else is exactly the gap that turns a clean headcount back into an unaccounted-for name.

title: Notify the plant's emergency dispatch
instruction: Call the plant's posted emergency contact and report the zone and the headcount.
rationale: Dispatch is the plan's own link to the responders who are actually equipped and trained to go back into that room — a call now with the zone and the headcount already in hand gets them moving with the facts, not guessing at them on arrival.

title: Raise the zone-mustered flag
instruction: Turn the flagpole crank to raise the flag showing your zone has fully mustered.
rationale: A raised flag is a fact a responder can see from across the lot without asking — it's the plan's own way of telling everyone arriving which zones are already accounted for and which still need a headcount taken.

title: Confirm the plan: no reentry before the all-clear
instruction: Read the posted plan and confirm what it asks: nobody goes back in until authorized personnel say so.
rationale: This is the one rule the entire response depends on — everything before this step only works if it's followed by nobody deciding, on their own judgment, that it's probably fine to go check.

title: Brief the responders on arrival
instruction: Point out the machine room entry first, then hand over the completed muster roster — in that order.
rationale: A responder arriving needs to know where to go before they need the paperwork — pointing them to the entry first gets them moving toward the actual problem while the roster, handed over right behind it, tells them exactly who is already accounted for.

title: Sign the incident log
instruction: Sign the log once responders have things in hand, closing out your part of the response.
rationale: The signature is your record of exactly what you did — read the panel, evacuated, mustered, notified — and it's the account a plant manager or an inspector reads afterward to understand how this response actually went.

situation: A coworker just behind you has turned around and is jogging back toward the machine room door, saying they forgot to shut something off.
instruction: They're heading the wrong way — get them turned back toward muster.
missed: They went back in before anyone stopped them. The muster roster now has a gap where their name should be, and the plan has no faster way to notice that gap than someone actually catching it before it happens.

situation: Someone unfamiliar with the plan has wandered up near the machine room and is reaching for the alarm panel to make the noise stop.
instruction: That panel is telling responders which zone still needs them — stop them before it goes quiet.
missed: The panel went quiet before responders ever arrived. Whatever they find when they get there, the one signal that told them exactly where to go first is now gone.

explanation: You wedged the machine room door open instead of letting it swing shut behind you. A door left open behind an ammonia leak is the leak's own path into the rest of the building, spreading past the one room built to contain it.

You're heading back in for a phone left on the bench. Nothing left inside that machine room is worth a single step back through that door once the alarm has sounded — the plan does not have an exception for a quick grab.

You reached to silence the alarm panel yourself. That panel is exactly what tells an arriving responder which zone still needs attention — silencing it because it's loud and inconvenient erases the one piece of information they're arriving to use.

You're walking back toward the machine room instead of continuing to muster. Every step back toward a room you just evacuated is a step the plan already told you not to take — the muster point is the only direction that matters right now.

title: Read the front-end shift board
instruction: Check your register assignment, your till start, and where the store's safety plan is posted.
rationale: The board is what tells you which stand is yours before you touch a single control on it, and it is where the store keeps the plan you are about to be trained on — reading it first means neither is a guess later in the shift.

title: Set the stand to fit you
instruction: Turn the stool's height adjustment until the belt sits at a neutral working height.
rationale: The Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation treats the height an object is lifted from as one of the biggest levers on injury risk, and a stand set too low or too high turns every single scan into a small reach that adds up across an eight-hour shift — set once, at the start, it protects every scan after it.

title: Hold a neutral scanning posture
instruction: Scan the practice items keeping your wrist straight and your elbow close, and hold it through the run.
rationale: A bent wrist repeated a few hundred times a shift is exactly the motion behind a lot of cashiers' own repetitive strain — a straight wrist and an elbow kept in close is the posture that costs nothing per scan and saves a joint over a career.

title: Lift the case with your legs, at a steady pace
instruction: Bend at the knees, keep the case close, and lift at a smooth, controlled rate.
rationale: A jerked lift asks your back to absorb a spike of force all at once; a smooth, controlled lift lets your legs — the muscles actually built for this — carry the load the whole way instead.

title: Call for a second hand on an awkward case
instruction: Page for bagging help before this case is lifted alone.
rationale: A case that is heavy and awkwardly shaped is exactly the load a second pair of hands turns from a twisted reach into a controlled two-person lift — calling for it costs a page, not calling for it can cost a shoulder.

title: Walk the front end before the doors open
instruction: Two things at this stand are wrong. Find them by looking.
rationale: Ergonomics is not only what happens at your own stand — a torn mat or a cord left where a cart can hide it is the same kind of injury waiting on somebody else's shift instead of yours.

title: Bag heavy items first
instruction: Bag the canned goods first, then the bread on top — in that order.
rationale: A bag packed heavy-on-top crushes whatever is underneath and throws its own balance off in a customer's hand — heavy low, light on top is the order that keeps the bag both intact and liftable.

title: Check ID on the age-restricted item
instruction: Scan the ID against the register's own prompt before this item rings through.
rationale: The register's own prompt is what this check runs against, per the store's policy — a cashier who rings it through without checking is the store's own compliance record, not just one transaction.

title: Locate the panic button
instruction: Find where the panic button actually is at your stand, per the store's posted plan.
rationale: Knowing exactly where this is before a shift ever needs it is the entire value of a store's safety plan — a cashier who has to search for it under pressure has already lost the seconds the plan was built to save.

title: Pull the till for a scheduled balance
instruction: Pull the till tray and move it to the secure drop slot for the scheduled mid-shift balance.
rationale: A scheduled balance keeps cash exposure at this stand capped through the shift instead of building toward one large count at close — the tray goes straight to the secure slot, not set down anywhere in between.

title: Confirm the store's plan: comply, don't chase
instruction: Read the posted plan and confirm what it asks of you if a demand for the register happens.
rationale: The store's own plan asks for exactly one thing in that moment: comply, and do not go after anyone once they have what they came for. Knowing that cold, before it is ever tested, is what keeps the moment from turning into a decision made on adrenaline instead of the plan.

title: Confirm when the alarm gets used
instruction: Confirm, per the plan, that the alarm is pressed once anyone involved has actually left — not before.
rationale: The store's plan times the alarm to after anyone involved is clear, because tripping it while they are still at the counter turns a resolved moment back into a live one, for you and for everyone else still in the store.

title: Run a mid-shift fatigue self-check
instruction: Rate your own posture and fatigue on the dial and commit once it's in the range that calls for a break.
rationale: A fatigue check partway through a shift is what catches the posture drift that happens gradually — nobody starts a shift slouched or twisting, and the dial is what makes noticing that a deliberate check instead of something only a sore back tells you about tomorrow.

title: Sign the shift safety check-in
instruction: Sign the log to close out this shift's ergonomics and safety check-in.
rationale: The signature is the cashier confirming the stand was set right, every heavy lift got called for help instead of twisted, and the plan was read — the record a supervisor checks if this stand's history is ever questioned.

situation: A coworker at the next stand is about to swing a heavy case off their own belt with a twist at the waist instead of turning their feet.
instruction: That's the exact motion this whole lifting technique exists to prevent — and it isn't your case.
missed: The twist happened before anyone said anything. The technique you just practiced only protects the person who actually uses it, and a coworker one stand over needed the same reminder you just got.

situation: A raised voice at the next lane over a price dispute has a brand-new cashier frozen, unsure what the store's plan even asks them to do.
instruction: They don't know where the plan starts — point them to it.
missed: The moment passed and the new cashier still doesn't know where the panic button is. The plan only protects the people who know it before they need it, and nobody just gave them that.

explanation: That cart is parked squarely across the front end's marked emergency exit. However full the lane gets, that path stays clear — it is the one route out of this room that does not run past the doors everyone else is using.

You came out from behind the stand to go after them. Once someone has what they came for, the incident is over — a cashier following a stranger into the parking lot alone turns one problem into a second one, voluntarily.

You reached for what's kept under the counter. Nothing at this stand is worth a physical confrontation — the store's plan exists precisely to take that choice off the table before anyone is ever tempted to make it.

You twisted at the waist to swing that case off the belt instead of turning your whole body. A twisted lift loads the spine sideways in a way it was never built for — turning your feet first is the entire difference between a heavy case and a strained back.

title: Read the allergen changeover card
instruction: Check what's coming off this slicer and what allergen the next order declares none of.
rationale: FDA 21 CFR 101 is why the major food allergens get named on a label at all, and the card is what tells you this changeover is a full allergen clean, not a routine wipe-down — the next customer's order depends on the difference being caught here, before the blade is even unplugged.

title: Unplug the slicer and lock the cord out
instruction: Pull the plug and clip your padlock through the cord-lockout device over the prongs.
rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 asks for the same promise here a breaker lock makes on a panel, sized for an appliance: the plug physically cannot go back in while your padlock is through it, so nobody — including you in a hurry — reconnects power before this clean is actually finished.

title: Break the slicer down in order
instruction: Lift the guard clear, then draw the carriage off its rail — in that order — onto the parts tray.
rationale: The carriage rides past the edge on every pass it makes, so it comes off only after the guard is already clear and the cord is already locked — there is no version of an allergen changeover where a hand is this close to the blade on a machine that could still be told to run.

title: Glove the cleaning hand
instruction: Pull the ANSI/ISEA-rated cut-resistant glove on before your hand goes near the blade.
rationale: Locking the cord out stops the blade from moving; it does not stop the blade from being a blade. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.138 is why the rated glove goes on for the one part of this changeover where a hand actually has to be beside the edge.

title: Wipe the blade edge-away
instruction: Fold the cloth flat and wipe outward from the centre, keeping clear of the edge, staying in the safe band.
rationale: Every trace of the last product has to come off this blade's face before an allergen changeover means anything, and it comes off wiped away from the edge with a folded cloth — stray too close and the wipe is grazing the one part of this machine still sharp with the guard sitting on a tray.

title: Sanitise the blade and bed, and hold contact time
instruction: Apply sanitiser to the blade face and slicing bed and hold for the full labelled contact time.
rationale: The sanitiser only earns its kill claim over its full labelled contact time, not the time it takes to feel done — an allergen changeover run short on this hold is a swab reading that only looks clean because nothing has actually been proven yet.

title: Swab the blade and bed for allergen protein
instruction: Run the ATP swab across the blade face and bed and commit once the reading is inside the clean band.
rationale: A clean-looking blade and a clean blade are not the same claim — the swab is what actually proves it for an allergen changeover, the way a look never can. A reading outside the clean band means the sanitiser step gets repeated, not argued with.

title: Walk the allergen line before it reopens
instruction: Two things on this line are wrong. Find them by looking.
rationale: The changeover isn't finished when the slicer swabs clean — it's finished when the whole line around it is as clean as the blade. Two things left wrong here become the next customer's undisclosed exposure, not just a tidiness note.

title: Rebuild the slicer in reverse
instruction: Seat the carriage back on the rail, then reseat the guard over the blade — in that order.
rationale: Reassembly runs teardown in reverse for a reason: a guard forced on before the carriage is square on its rail can bind against it, and a bound part now is a part somebody forces later under load.

title: Prove the guard interlock
instruction: Bump the power switch with the guard seated and confirm the motor is live only now.
rationale: The interlock is what should have kept this slicer from running the entire time the guard was off, and testing it after reassembly — guard seated, before the lock comes off — is the only way to know it still does that job.

title: Remove your lock from the cord
instruction: Take your padlock off the cord-lockout device now that the slicer is fully reassembled and proven.
rationale: Your lock, your call — nobody else removes it, and it comes off only once the interlock is proven and every part is back where it belongs.

title: Plug the slicer back in
instruction: Seat the plug fully into the outlet, last, after everything else is done.
rationale: Power comes back to this machine exactly once in this whole changeover, and it's the very last thing that happens — after the guard, after the interlock test, after your own lock is off.

title: Flip the line's allergen placard
instruction: Turn the placard holder to show the correct allergen declaration for what's coming next.
rationale: The placard is what tells the next clerk, and the customer standing at the case, what this line has and has not touched — leaving yesterday's declaration up is a wrong answer with a confident sign behind it.

title: Sign the allergen changeover log
instruction: Sign the log to close out the allergen changeover.
rationale: The signature is the clerk taking responsibility for the whole changeover — locked, cleaned, swabbed clean, placard flipped — and it is the record a manager reads if this line's history is ever questioned.

situation: A coworker has picked up the one scoop off the counter and is about to dip it in the peanut-declared bin, then the one right next to it.
instruction: That scoop is on its way to being in both bins in the same minute.
missed: The scoop went into both bins before anyone stopped it. Whatever cross-contact your changeover just proved clean on the slicer, the bins next to it just undid with a single scoop.

situation: A second clerk has grabbed the slicer's cord and is reaching for the outlet — a rush order just came in and they haven't clocked your lock.
instruction: Your hand is on the blade and somebody is about to give it power.
missed: They plugged it in with your hand still at the blade. The lock was doing its job right up until somebody didn't look for it — a cord-lockout only protects the person who makes sure it gets seen.

explanation: You touched the mounted blade's edge directly to check it. Gloved or not, a fingertip is never how this edge gets checked — a folded cloth held flat against the face of the blade tells you everything a touch would, without an edge anywhere near your skin.

That bin's allergen placard is missing and its lid is off. An open, unlabelled bin next to product with none of that allergen in it is exactly how a declared ingredient ends up in an order nobody warned about.

That's the one scoop sitting between both bins — the peanut-declared salad and the one next to it with none in it. A scoop that touches one bin and then the other carries the allergen across on contact alone; each bin gets its own scoop, always, not whichever one is closest.

That's the panini press's cord, not the slicer's. Locking out the wrong plug leaves this blade fully live while your hands are inside the guard — the tag in your hand has to match the machine you're standing at, every time.

title: Read the changeover ticket
instruction: Check what the case needs next and confirm both machines are between runs, not mid-cut.
rationale: The ticket says what is coming off the saw and into the grinder next, and confirming both machines are actually stopped before touching either one is the first fact this whole teardown depends on — starting a lockout on a saw that is still finishing a cut is how a hand ends up where a blade already is.

title: Glove and guard up
instruction: Pull on the mesh glove, then buckle the belly guard over it — in that order.
rationale: ANSI/ISEA 105 rates the mesh glove for exactly this job, and OSHA 29 CFR 1910.138 is why it goes on before anything else — the belly guard buckles over the glove's cuff, not under it, so a slipped blade meets the guard before it ever reaches the wrist the glove stops at.

title: Lock out the band saw's disconnect
instruction: Open the band saw's own disconnect switch and clip your padlock through it.
rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 asks for one thing before any guard comes off a powered machine: the energy source isolated and locked by the person about to work on it. This switch is wired to the saw alone, so your lock here — and nowhere else — is what keeps that motor from being told to run while your hands are inside it.

title: Test the motor leads for zero energy
instruction: Touch the non-contact tester to the motor leads and commit once it reads dead.
rationale: A locked switch is a promise, not a proof — the tester is what actually confirms the promise held. OSHA 1910.147 calls this the try step for a reason: a breaker that was mislabelled, or a lock clipped on the wrong hasp, only shows up here, before the guard comes off, not after.

title: Remove the wheel guard
instruction: Lift the upper wheel guard clear and set it on the parts tray.
rationale: The guard comes off only after the saw is proven dead — reaching for it before that tests a hope, not a lock. Off, it goes straight onto the tray in the order it will go back on, so reassembly starts from a sequence instead of a guess.

title: Slip the band blade off the wheels
instruction: Release the tension handle and draw the blade off both wheels onto the tray.
rationale: The blade rides both wheels under real tension, and it comes off only once that tension is released and the guard is already clear — pulling a tensioned blade off a wheel with a hand still inside the housing is exactly the motion this whole lockout exists to prevent.

title: Walk the saw before it goes back together
instruction: Two things on this machine are wrong. Find them before reassembly starts.
rationale: The teardown is not finished when the guard and blade are off — it is finished when the machine underneath them is checked, not just wiped. Two things left wrong here become the next shift's surprise, or the health inspector's.

title: Sanitise the table, guides and wheel wells
instruction: Spray the food-contact surfaces and hold for the full labelled contact time.
rationale: NSF/ANSI 8 governs this machine as food-contact equipment for a reason — whatever rode the last cut across this table is what the next customer's dinner touches if it is not actually killed, and a sanitiser only earns that claim over its full contact time, not the time it takes to feel done.

title: Seat the band blade back on the wheels
instruction: Return the blade from the tray onto both wheels and tension it true.
rationale: Reassembly runs the teardown in reverse for a reason: a blade forced onto the wheels before the guard is anywhere near ready can walk off-track under tension, and a blade that walks under load is one nobody wants to be standing beside.

title: Reseat the wheel guard
instruction: Set the guard back over the wheel housing and seat it flush.
rationale: A guard that looks back in place and a guard that is actually seated are not the same thing — it has to sit flush against the housing so the interlock behind it can even close, which is what the next step is there to prove.

title: Prove the guard interlock
instruction: Bump the test switch with the guard seated and confirm the motor is live only now.
rationale: The interlock should have kept this saw from running the entire time the guard was off, and testing it after reassembly — guard seated, before your lock comes off — is the only way to know it still does that job before this machine sees a primal again.

title: Unplug the grinder and lock the cord out
instruction: Pull the grinder's plug and clip your padlock through the cord-lockout device.
rationale: The grinder gets its own lock on its own cord, separate from the saw — a device with a single auger and a knife spinning at the bottom of an open hopper does not get a hand near it on a hope that somebody else already unplugged it.

title: Remove the grinder's feed pan and stomper guard
instruction: Lift the feed pan and stomper guard clear and set them on the parts tray.
rationale: The feed pan sits directly over the worm that feeds the knife and plate, and it comes off only once the cord is out and locked — the same promise the saw's own lockout just made, sized for a machine you feed by hand instead of a blade you guide by eye.

title: Remove your locks
instruction: Take both of your padlocks off the lock board now that each machine is proven and reassembled.
rationale: Your locks, your call — nobody else takes them off, and neither comes off until its own machine is fully back together and proven. Pulling either one early hands live power back to a machine somebody else might still have a hand inside.

title: Sign the changeover log
instruction: Sign the log to close out the between-use clean on both machines.
rationale: The signature is the cutter taking responsibility for the whole changeover — both machines locked, both cleaned, both proven — and it is the line a manager or an inspector reads when either machine's history is ever questioned.

situation: A second cutter has walked up to the saw's disconnect box, reaching to flip it back on for the next order — they have not clocked your lock.
instruction: Your hand is inside the wheel housing and somebody is about to give this saw power.
missed: They flipped the switch with your hand still inside the wheel housing. The lock was doing its job right up until somebody didn't look for it first — a disconnect lockout only protects the person who makes sure it gets noticed.

situation: A stock clerk has wheeled a cart of trim scraps up to the grinder and is about to tip it straight into the open hopper.
instruction: That hopper has no feed pan on it and no proof this grinder is even locked out to anyone but you.
missed: The trim went into the open hopper before the grinder was proven, guarded or reassembled. Whatever was in that scoop is now mixed into a machine somebody else believed was ready — because nothing here told them it wasn't.

explanation: You touched the band blade's edge directly to feel for nicks. That edge runs the full loop between both wheels with nothing covering it once the guard is off — a folded cloth held flat against the flat of the blade tells you everything a fingertip would, without an edge anywhere near your skin.

That switch is the guard interlock's manual override, wired in for a mechanic's bench test — not a between-use clean. Flipping it lets the wheel housing sit open while the motor can still be told to run, which defeats the one thing standing between this blade and the hand reaching in to wipe it down.

That spare band blade is coiled on the hook with no sheath over its edge. A band blade has no dull side to carry it by — it goes up in its guard or it does not come off that hook bare-handed at all, whatever is waiting on the saw.

That is the walk-in condenser's own disconnect, not the saw's — the two boxes sit side by side on this wall and look almost identical. Locking out the wrong one leaves the band saw's motor fully live while your hands are inside the wheel housing; the tag in your hand has to match the machine you are standing at, every single time.

title: Read the line assignment board
instruction: Check your station on the line and today's rotation schedule before anything else.
rationale: The board is what tells you which cut this station makes and when your rotation comes around — starting without reading it means guessing at both, on a line that does not slow down to let you catch up.

title: Don PPE in order
instruction: Glove, then sleeve over its cuff, then the belly-guard apron over both — in that order.
rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.138 and ANSI/ISEA 105 rate each piece on its own, but the order is what makes them work together: the sleeve overlaps the glove's cuff, and the apron overlaps the sleeve, so there is no gap between them for an edge to find.

title: Check out your knife
instruction: Sign your knife out of the crib for this shift, per the plant's own tool-control procedure.
rationale: A knife accounted for at check-out is a knife accounted for at check-in — tool control on a cutting line is what tells the next shift, and an inspector, that every blade issued today is a blade that came back.

title: Hone the edge before the first cut
instruction: Draw the blade down the steel at a steady angle and hold it through the full pass count.
rationale: A honed edge needs less force to make the same cut than a dull one does, and less force behind a knife is less force behind a slip. Honing before the first cut, not after the knife starts fighting the product, is what keeps that force low all shift.

title: Check the line speed against its posted band
instruction: Read the line speed indicator and commit once it's inside the posted safe band for this cut.
rationale: The posted band is the plant's own answer to how fast this specific cut can be made safely, and it's checked before the first product reaches your station, not discovered by falling behind on the third one.

title: Walk the station before the line starts
instruction: Two things at this station are wrong. Find them before the first product arrives.
rationale: A changeover isn't finished when your own PPE is on — it's finished when the station around you is checked too. Two things left wrong here become the next cutter's surprise, not just yours.

title: Practice a controlled cutting stroke
instruction: Draw the blade through a controlled stroke length — not a cramped one, not an overreach.
rationale: A cramped stroke forces you to reposition constantly, and an overreach puts your off-hand closer to the blade's path than it needs to be — a controlled, consistent stroke length is the one that repeats safely a few hundred times a shift.

title: Pass the knife handle-first
instruction: Set the knife handle-first on the pass tray for the next cutter, never handed edge-out.
rationale: The pass tray is what takes the handoff out of two hands entirely — a knife set down handle-first and picked up handle-first never has a moment where the blade is pointed at anybody's hand but the person already holding it.

title: Request a line-speed adjustment
instruction: Turn the request dial to call for the line to slow to the posted band, not past it.
rationale: The request dial is the line's own control for exactly this moment — falling behind the cut in front of you is a reason to call for the posted band to be held, not a reason to rush the next several cuts to catch back up.

title: Dip the knife between tasks
instruction: Drop the knife into the sanitising dip station between cuts on different product.
rationale: A blade carries whatever it last cut into the next one it touches — the dip station between tasks is what keeps one product's contact time from becoming the next product's contamination.

title: Take your scheduled rotation
instruction: Check the rotation board and move to your next assigned task on schedule.
rationale: The rotation exists because the same motion repeated for a whole shift is what builds a repetitive strain injury nobody feels coming — taking it on schedule, not skipping it for one more cycle, is the entire point of it being scheduled at all.

title: Return your knife to the crib
instruction: Sign your knife back into the crib at the end of your task on this station.
rationale: The knife that left the crib with your name on it is the same knife that has to come back with your name on it — tool control only works if the return happens every time, not just when nothing else is going on.

title: Wash hands and tools between line changes
instruction: Wash your hands and the sanitised tools and hold through the full wash count.
rationale: A line change is a contact-time reset for your hands, not just your knife — a wash cut short leaves the last task's residue riding into the next one on the one tool nobody else double-checks.

title: Sign the line log
instruction: Sign the log to close out this changeover.
rationale: The signature is the cutter taking responsibility for the whole changeover — knife issued and returned, PPE donned in order, rotation taken — and it's the record a supervisor reads if this station's history is ever questioned.

situation: A coworker is walking up holding their knife out blade-first, about to hand it to you directly instead of using the tray.
instruction: That handoff has a blade pointed at your hand the whole way across.
missed: The handoff happened hand to hand, blade-first, before anyone redirected it. Whatever training says about the tray, a habit only holds up if it gets used the one time somebody skips it in a hurry.

situation: The line has visibly sped up past the posted band, and product is starting to stack up in front of your station.
instruction: That's a reason to request the band back, not a reason to rush the next several cuts.
missed: The rushed cuts kept pace with the line, not with the stroke you were trained to hold. Speed gained here is exactly the kind that shows up later as a slip nobody saw building.

explanation: That knife is sitting blade-first, handle away, the way it should never be picked up or handed off. A blade passed or reached for edge-first hands the next set of fingers the one part of it that cuts, first.

That knife on the rail is visibly nicked and dulled, and it's tempting to press down harder with it rather than swap it out. A dull edge needs more downward force to make the same cut, and force is exactly what turns a slip into a laceration on a line moving at a set pace.

You cranked the speed request dial past the posted band instead of calling for a slower line. Running ahead of the band you were trained to work inside of is how a controlled cut turns into a rushed one, every single time the line is running faster than the cut in front of it.

That station down the line has no mesh glove hanging at it — somebody is cutting without one. A cut-resistant glove that stays on its hook instead of a hand is exactly the gap ANSI/ISEA 105's rating was never going to close by itself.

title: Read tonight's stocking manifest
instruction: Check the pallet list for the overnight shift and confirm the baler and compactor are between cycles.
rationale: The manifest sets what gets broken down and baled tonight, and confirming both machines are actually between cycles before touching either one is the fact this whole shift's safety depends on — starting a lockout on a baler mid-cycle is how a hand ends up where a ram already is.

title: Flatten and queue the cardboard
instruction: Break the empty box down flat, then stack it in the queue at the baler's infeed — in that order.
rationale: A box broken down flat feeds the chamber evenly; one still half-folded is exactly the kind of load that jams a ram halfway through its stroke. Queuing it at the infeed, not shoving it straight into a running chamber, is what keeps hands clear of the machine doing the actual work.

title: Notice the baler's jam light
instruction: Check the amber jam indicator on the baler's control panel before feeding it anything else.
rationale: The jam light is the machine telling you the ram stalled mid-stroke — feeding more cardboard into a chamber that already has a jammed load in it only packs the jam in tighter, and it is the last normal-looking thing this baler does before somebody's hand goes in after it.

title: Lock out the baler's disconnect
instruction: Open the baler's own disconnect switch and clip your padlock through it.
rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 asks for one thing before any hand goes near a jammed ram: the energy source isolated and locked by the person about to clear it. This switch is wired to the baler alone, so your lock — and nowhere else — is what keeps that ram from being told to finish its stroke.

title: Test the control circuit for zero energy
instruction: Touch the tester to the baler's control leads and commit once it reads dead.
rationale: A locked switch is a promise; the tester is what proves it. ANSI B11's own machinery-safety approach and 1910.147 both ask for this exact step before a guard or a gate ever opens on a machine that was just running — it is where a mislabelled breaker shows up, not after.

title: Draw the jammed cardboard out
instruction: Pull the jammed wad out of the chamber at a slow, steady rate — too fast snags it on the ram.
rationale: A jam under real tension does not come free with one hard yank — it comes free at a steady pull that lets the wad clear the ram's edge instead of tearing and re-wedging against it, the same way it jammed in the first place.

title: Walk the baler before it closes back up
instruction: Two things at this machine are wrong. Find them before the gate closes.
rationale: Clearing the jam isn't the end of this — the machine underneath it gets checked, not just cleared. Two things left wrong here become the next shift's surprise, or worse, the next jam somebody reaches into believing it is only a jam.

title: Prove the gate interlock
instruction: Bump the test switch with the gate closed and read the control circuit, committing once it shows live.
rationale: The interlock is what should have kept this baler from cycling the entire time the gate was open, and reading the control circuit after reassembly is the only way to know it still does that job before this machine takes another load.

title: Remove your lock from the baler
instruction: Take your padlock off the baler's disconnect now that the jam is cleared and the interlock is proven.
rationale: Your lock, your call — nobody else removes it, and it comes off only once the gate is closed, the interlock is proven and the chamber is actually clear.

title: Lock out the cardboard compactor
instruction: Open the compactor's own disconnect and clip your padlock through it before the hopper is touched.
rationale: The compactor's ram crushes its own load without any warning stroke, and it gets its own lock on its own disconnect — a hand does not go into that hopper on the hope that somebody already shut it off.

title: Open the compactor's inspection gate
instruction: Swing the ram chamber's inspection gate open and set it against its stop.
rationale: The gate opens only after the disconnect is locked — reaching for it before that tests a hope, not a lock, on a ram built to crush cardboard without ever needing to know a hand replaced it.

title: Close the gate and remove your compactor lock
instruction: Swing the gate shut and take your padlock off the compactor's disconnect.
rationale: The gate closes before the lock comes off, not after — a compactor with its lock removed and its gate still open is a live ram with nothing between it and whoever walks by next.

title: Tension and tie the finished bale
instruction: Turn the wire tensioner down until the bale holds its shape on its own.
rationale: A bale tied loose comes apart the first time it is moved, and a bale tensioned unevenly can snap a wire under load — turning the tensioner to a steady, even tension is what makes this bale safe to stage and safe for whoever loads it next.

title: Stage the bale for pickup
instruction: Move the finished, tied bale to the marked staging area by the dock door.
rationale: A finished bale left in the aisle behind the baler is a blind-corner obstacle for the next stocker pushing a loaded pallet jack through — staging it at the marked area keeps the whole backroom aisle clear for what still has to move through it tonight.

title: Sign the maintenance log
instruction: Sign the log to close out tonight's jam-clearing on both machines.
rationale: The signature is the stocker taking responsibility for the whole procedure — both machines locked, cleared and proven — and it is the line the day manager reads if either machine's history is ever questioned.

situation: A new stocker has walked up to the baler's start button, about to bump it to "see if it's still stuck" — they haven't clocked your lock on the disconnect.
instruction: Your hand is inside the chamber and somebody is about to try starting this baler.
missed: They bumped the start button with your hand still inside the chamber. The lock was doing its job right up until somebody didn't look for it first — a disconnect lockout only protects the person who makes sure it gets noticed.

situation: A coworker has wheeled a cart of broken-down boxes up to the compactor and is about to tip them straight into the open hopper.
instruction: That hopper's gate is open for an inspection, not for a load — nobody has proven this machine is locked out to anyone but you.
missed: The boxes went into the hopper before the compactor was closed back up and proven. Whatever was in that cart is now sitting against a ram somebody else believed was ready to run — because nothing here told them it wasn't.

explanation: You're reaching into the compactor hopper to free the jam with the ram's own power still live. A cardboard compactor's ram is built to crush its own load without warning; the hopper only gets a hand inside it once the unit is proven locked out, never before.

The gate's own limit-switch wire is frayed down to bare copper. A limit switch that can short or fail open is a guard interlock the machine cannot actually trust, whatever the gate itself looks like from the outside.

That baler chamber has no lock on its disconnect. Reaching into a jammed chamber that could still be told to cycle is the single most common way a baler-related injury actually happens in a grocery backroom — the ram does not know a hand is where the cardboard was.

That danger tag on the panel is from a shift that ended hours ago, with nobody's name on this shift's own lockout log. An unaccounted-for lock or tag left on a panel is exactly what group lockout procedures exist to prevent — every lock on that panel has to belong to somebody working right now.

title: Check the chemical inventory board
instruction: Compare what's on the shelf against today's inventory list for both departments.
rationale: The inventory board is the only record of what's actually supposed to be on these shelves — a chemical that shows up without a line on the board is one nobody has checked against an SDS yet, and that gets caught here, not after it's already stored.

title: Look up the SDS before handling anything
instruction: Pull the safety data sheet for the chemical you're about to store or mix.
rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 puts the SDS at the centre of hazard communication for exactly this reason — it's the one document that tells you the storage, handling and first-aid facts for this specific chemical, checked before the container is opened, not guessed at from the label's front panel.

title: Glove and goggle up
instruction: Pull on the chemical-resistant gloves, then the splash goggles — in that order.
rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.138 and 1910.133 rate each piece for a different part of the same splash — gloves first so your hands are already covered by the time you reach for the goggles, not the other way around.

title: Check the storage compatibility chart
instruction: Check the chart before shelving this chemical anywhere near what's already stored.
rationale: A compatibility chart is what turns "there's room on this shelf" into an actual answer about whether two chemicals belong near each other — an acid and a base sharing a shelf because there was space is exactly the gap this chart exists to close.

title: Move the incompatible container
instruction: Move the container that failed the compatibility check to its own segregated shelf.
rationale: A container that fails the compatibility chart doesn't get left where it is because moving it is inconvenient — it goes to the shelf built for exactly this, right away, not on the next slow afternoon.

title: Walk the chemical storage before it's touched
instruction: Two things in this storage area are wrong. Find them by looking.
rationale: A chemical storage check isn't finished when the shelf looks organised — it's finished when every container on it is actually sound and actually identifiable. Two things left wrong here become the next clerk's exposure.

title: Mix the floral preservative to the label
instruction: Meter the concentrate into the water and commit once the mix is at the label's own ratio.
rationale: The label's ratio is the only number this mix is measured against — too weak and the preservative does nothing for the flowers it's meant to protect, too strong and it's an unnecessary chemical exposure for whoever handles the buckets next.

title: Apply the spill kit per the SDS
instruction: Open the spill kit and apply the absorbent, holding it down for the SDS's own dwell guidance.
rationale: The spill kit's absorbent only does its job over the dwell time the SDS actually calls for — lifting it early leaves exactly the residue underneath that the kit was supposed to take care of.

title: Sweep the residue at a controlled pace
instruction: Sweep the absorbed residue toward the containment bag at a slow, controlled pace.
rationale: A fast sweep flings residue outward past the containment area you just set up — a slow, controlled pass keeps everything the spill kit already absorbed inside the area meant to hold it.

title: Confirm the eyewash is clear and functional
instruction: Check that the path to the eyewash is clear and the unit activates.
rationale: An eyewash confirmed clear before a chemical is even opened is what makes the ten seconds after a real splash a routine flush instead of a search for a station nobody checked was working.

title: Turn on the back-room ventilation
instruction: Turn the ventilation fan switch on before working with the concentrate, per the SDS's guidance.
rationale: The SDS's own ventilation guidance exists because a concentrate's fumes build up fastest in exactly the small back room this work happens in — the fan runs before the container opens, not after somebody notices the air feels wrong.

title: Dispose of the spill materials properly
instruction: Move the used spill kit materials to the hazardous waste container, not the regular trash.
rationale: Absorbent that just took up a chemical is not regular trash anymore — the SDS's own disposal guidance is what tells you it goes to a hazardous waste container, and skipping that step just relocates the exposure instead of ending it.

title: Log the spill
instruction: Fill out the incident form for the spill before the shift moves on.
rationale: A spill that isn't logged is a spill the next shift has no way of knowing happened — the form is what turns a cleaned-up mess into a record somebody can actually act on if it happens again.

title: Sign the chemical handling log
instruction: Sign the log to close out today's chemical handling check.
rationale: The signature is the clerk taking responsibility for the whole check — every chemical inventoried, checked against its SDS, stored compatibly and any spill logged — and it's the record read if either department's chemical handling is ever questioned.

situation: A coworker is about to pour a different floral chemical straight into your mixed preservative bucket to save a second trip to the shelf.
instruction: That's two chemicals about to combine with nobody having checked compatibility.
missed: The pour happened before anyone checked the chart. Whatever that combination does, nobody standing there actually knew it was safe before it happened — which is exactly what the chart was there to answer.

situation: Someone from another department is walking straight toward the spill area, unaware it's an active chemical cleanup.
instruction: Get them behind the barrier before they walk through it.
missed: They walked through the spill area before anyone redirected them. Whatever was in that spill, it's now on a second person's shoes, tracked toward wherever they were headed.

explanation: Those cases are stacked directly in front of the eyewash station. An eyewash that takes ten seconds to reach because of a delivery nobody moved yet is an eyewash that misses the one window that actually matters after a splash.

You're about to pour that returned cleaner straight into the floral preservative bucket to save a trip to the shelf. Two chemicals with no checked compatibility do not get combined on a guess — the SDS for each one is what tells you whether that's a reaction waiting to happen, not how full the bucket looks.

You're reaching for the concentrate with no eye protection on. The splash risk on a concentrate is exactly what OSHA 29 CFR 1910.133 rates eye protection for — the goggles go on before the cap comes off, not after something already went wrong.

That spray bottle has no label on it at all. A decanted chemical with nothing written on the bottle is a chemical nobody after you can identify — OSHA's hazard communication rule exists because the one thing worse than a hazardous chemical is one nobody can name in an emergency.

title: Check the invoice against the order
instruction: Compare the delivery invoice to today's produce order before the truck is unloaded.
rationale: The invoice is the only record of what was supposed to arrive, at what count. Catching a shortage or a substitution here is a phone call to the supplier; catching it after the truck has left is a credit dispute nobody can prove.

title: Read the truck's reefer display
instruction: Read the truck's own reefer temperature through the window and commit once it shows the load has held cold the whole trip.
rationale: The reefer display is the truck's own record of the whole trip, not just the last few minutes at your dock. A trailer reading warm before the door is even open has already failed the delivery, whatever the first case you probe happens to read.

title: Open the truck and bridge the dock
instruction: Open the truck doors, then bridge the gap with the dock leveler — in that order.
rationale: The doors open onto a load that has been sealed and refrigerated for hours; the leveler only bridges a gap you can actually see once the doors are open. Dropping the leveler onto closed doors tells you nothing about the load behind them.

title: Confirm the trailer's wheel chocks
instruction: Check that both wheel chocks are seated against the trailer's tires before anyone works the dock plate.
rationale: A trailer with no tractor still attached can creep away from the dock under its own weight, and the gap that opens between the trailer and the leveler is exactly where a loaded pallet jack goes down. The chocks are what keep that gap from ever opening while the dock is in use.

title: Probe the leafy greens case
instruction: Probe between two heads in the leafy greens case and commit once the reading is inside the store's posted cold range.
rationale: Leafy greens show field heat and cold-chain gaps faster than almost anything else on this pallet, so probing between two heads — not the outside of the case where the trailer's air has been blowing on it — is what actually tells you whether this delivery held its temperature the whole trip.

title: Walk the pallet for damage before it's accepted
instruction: Two things on this pallet are not sound. Find them before anything is accepted.
rationale: Produce is checked with your hands and your eyes on every case, not sampled on a few — a crushed flat or a spoiled bag left in place keeps doing damage to everything stacked around it for as long as it sits there.

title: Check the ethylene segregation chart
instruction: Check the chart before the pallet is broken down, to see what has to be kept apart from what.
rationale: Ethylene-producing produce and ethylene-sensitive produce riding the same pallet face to face is a fast way to have half a delivery ripening before it reaches the case — the chart is what tells you which is which before the segregation happens, not after a customer notices.

title: Cull the failed case
instruction: Pull the crushed berry flat and move it to the reject zone.
rationale: A culled case leaves the delivery physically, right away — set beside the accepted pallet, it is one distracted moment away from riding to the walk-in with everything else.

title: Log the cull
instruction: Write the item, the reason and the quantity culled on the refusal log.
rationale: The refusal log is what gets a credit from the supplier and tells the next shift why a case on the invoice never made it to the floor. Without it, a cull is just missing inventory nobody can explain.

title: Strap the pallet jack's load
instruction: Ratchet the strap down over the stacked accepted cases before the jack ever moves.
rationale: A stack that shifts on a moving pallet jack comes down on whoever is driving it, not on the floor first. The strap is what turns a stack of separate cases into one load that goes exactly where the jack points it.

title: Drive the load to the walk-in
instruction: Sound the horn at both blind corners and hold a steady, balanced pace the whole way to the walk-in door.
rationale: The backroom aisle to the walk-in runs past two blind corners a stock clerk could step around at any moment, and a pallet jack loaded to eye height cannot be stopped the way a person on foot can. The horn is what buys the half-second a corner does not give you any other way.

title: Read the walk-in's own thermometer
instruction: Read the walk-in cooler's posted thermometer and commit once it shows the room is inside its own range.
rationale: The delivery's cold chain is not actually unbroken until the room it lands in is proven cold too — a probe that passed at the dock means nothing if the pallet is about to sit inside a walk-in that has been running warm all shift.

title: Rotate the stock by date
instruction: Check the FIFO card and place the new pallet behind whatever produce is already in the walk-in.
rationale: First in, first out only works if the newest pallet actually goes behind the oldest one every single time — put it in front because it's closer to the door, and the case in back is what a clerk finds spoiled next week.

title: Sign the receiving log
instruction: Sign the receiving log to close out the delivery.
rationale: The signature is the clerk taking responsibility for every reading on this delivery — what was accepted, what was culled and why, and what the walk-in itself read when the pallet went inside.

situation: The driver has climbed back into the cab and is revving the engine — two more stops on the route, and the chocks haven't even been checked yet.
instruction: This trailer does not get treated as parked until the chocks are actually confirmed.
missed: You let the driver's hurry carry the moment and never confirmed the chocks. If that trailer had crept even a few inches with a hand truck on the plate, the schedule that pressured you would not have been the thing anyone remembered.

situation: A stock clerk has grabbed the culled berry flat off the reject zone by mistake and is wheeling it toward the walk-in with the rest of the order.
instruction: Stop that case before it reaches the walk-in — it already failed inspection.
missed: The culled case went into the walk-in with everything else. It now reads, to every clerk who opens that door, exactly like every other case on the shelf — the refusal log sitting back on the dock is the only thing that ever said otherwise.

explanation: You waved the truck off without reading the reefer display. A trailer that has been running warm on the road has already started this delivery behind, and produce that spent the trip too warm does not recover once it is inside a cold walk-in.

That banana case is stacked flush against the leafy greens. Bananas are one of the produce department's own heaviest ethylene producers, and stacking one against an ethylene-sensitive case starts ripening — and yellowing — the case next to it before it ever reaches the floor.

You propped the walk-in door open with the pallet instead of closing it behind you. A propped cooler door is a slow, continuous temperature excursion for every case already inside it, not just the one you are wheeling through.

You drove the loaded jack straight across the wet, icy patch on the apron instead of matting or clearing it first. A dock apron gets wet from every reefer that runs and every case that drips, and OSHA's walking-working-surfaces rule exists because that surface takes a loaded pallet jack down as easily as it takes a person.

title: Read the interceptor's service card
instruction: Check the unit's size, its last service date and the FOG programme's service interval before opening anything.
rationale: The service card is what ties this specific unit to the FOG programme's permit conditions — the interval, the manifest requirement and the 25 percent rule all apply because this card says this interceptor is on that programme, not because the lid happens to look due.

title: Answer the confined-space question
instruction: Read the decision flowchart and confirm this under-sink interceptor is not a permit-required confined space.
rationale: OSHA 1910.146 asks whether a space is entered bodily and whether it can develop a hazardous atmosphere or trap someone — this small under-counter unit is serviced entirely from the top opening with nobody's body ever going inside it, which is a different call from the outdoor in-ground interceptor a hauler's crew actually climbs down into. Answering it here, not assuming it, is what keeps a routine task routine.

title: Glove, apron and goggle up
instruction: Gloves, apron and splash goggles before the lid comes off.
rationale: What's under that lid is decomposing food waste and grease that has been sitting for days — the gloves keep it off your hands, the apron keeps it off your clothes, and the goggles are what stand between your eyes and whatever comes up when the lid finally breaks its seal.

title: Set up ventilation before opening the lid
instruction: Position the portable fan to move air across the opening before you break the seal.
rationale: A closed interceptor traps whatever gas the waste inside it has been producing, and moving air across the opening before the lid comes off is what keeps that gas from simply pooling around whoever is kneeling over it a minute later.

title: Lift the lid with the hook tool
instruction: Hook the tool into the lid's lift eye and break the seal — never with your fingers.
rationale: A grease-sealed cast-iron lid does not lift smoothly; it holds and then releases all at once. The hook tool keeps every one of your fingers away from the gap that is about to open, which your bare hand cannot promise you.

title: Pause over the open lid before reaching in
instruction: Hold back from the opening, look and smell for anything wrong before your hands go anywhere near it.
rationale: The open lid is the one moment in this whole service where an atmosphere problem would actually show itself — a held pause here is a five-second check against exactly the kind of surprise the confined-space call assumed would not need a permit to manage.

title: Measure the grease and solids against the 25 percent rule
instruction: Dip the measuring stick to the bottom and commit the combined grease-and-solids reading as a share of the total liquid depth.
rationale: The interceptor is due for pumping once the combined grease cap and settled solids reach about a quarter of the unit's total liquid depth — past that point the trap is losing the working volume it needs to actually separate anything, and it starts passing grease straight through to the line it is supposed to protect.

title: Check the baffles and flow control
instruction: Look at the internal baffle wall and the flow-control fitting before pumping anything out.
rationale: The baffles and the flow control are what actually make this a grease interceptor instead of a plain tank — a cracked baffle or a blocked fitting means the unit has been passing grease through even while every reading on the outside looked normal.

title: Pump the contents to the sealed container
instruction: Hold the vacuum hose steady into the sealed haul container, never toward the floor drain.
rationale: The whole point of a sealed container is that grease waste leaves this kitchen as a manifested load a hauler is responsible for, not as whatever ran down the nearest drain — a hose that wanders off the container for even a few seconds puts waste exactly where the FOG programme exists to keep it from going.

title: Seal the haul container
instruction: Close and latch the container's lid once the pump-out is finished.
rationale: A sealed container is what keeps this load a controlled shipment instead of an open tub of grease sitting in a kitchen until the hauler shows up — sealed now, it stays that way through however long it waits by the back door.

title: Rinse the interior
instruction: Hold the rinse wand over the baffles and walls until the residue is gone.
rationale: Grease left clinging to the baffles and walls after a pump-out is grease that is already back at work re-coating the unit before it is even resealed — the rinse is what actually resets the trap to empty rather than just lower.

title: Reseat and torque the lid
instruction: Turn the locking ring until the lid seats flush and the bolts are snug.
rationale: A lid that is set back on but not actually torqued down is a lid that can be lifted by the next pressure surge in the line, or by a foot that catches its edge — the bolts are what turn a resting cover back into a sealed access point.

title: Complete the hauler's manifest
instruction: Fill in the volume, the date and your signature on the manifest before the hauler takes the container.
rationale: The manifest is what makes this load traceable from your kitchen to wherever the hauler actually takes it — under the FOG programme, a grease shipment with no manifest is treated the same as one that never left through the proper route at all.

title: Log the service for inspection
instruction: Record the date, the reading and the volume pumped in the maintenance log.
rationale: The utility's FOG inspectors check this log against the interceptor's permitted service interval — a trap that is actually maintained on schedule but has no log to prove it gets treated exactly like one that was never serviced at all.

situation: A rotten-egg smell rolls up out of the open interceptor the moment the lid comes off — stronger than the usual grease odour.
instruction: That smell is hydrogen sulphide. Back off the opening and get air moving before anyone goes near it again.
missed: Somebody stayed leaning over the open lid breathing whatever that smell was instead of stepping back and letting the fan clear it — the smell not getting stronger is not the same thing as the gas not being there.

situation: Across the kitchen, a line cook is tipping a pan of spent fryer oil straight down the prep sink instead of into the grease jug by the fryer.
instruction: Stop her before that oil hits the drain — that's exactly what this interceptor is trying to keep up with.
missed: The oil went down the drain while the trap you were servicing sat open on the floor a few feet away — the FOG programme's own numbers assume that oil goes in a jug, not down a sink, and this shift just broke that assumption.

explanation: You went at that lid with your bare hands instead of the hook tool. A grease-sealed lid lets go all at once when it finally breaks free, and a hand caught under a cast-iron lid coming down is a crushed finger before anyone has even started the actual service.

That overflow line runs straight to the kitchen's floor drain instead of the sealed haul container. Grease down a drain is exactly what this interceptor exists to stop — and it is also a direct violation of the FOG programme this unit is permitted under.

That's an open flame next to an interceptor that has been sitting closed and building gas off decomposing grease. Trapped organic waste generates methane, and an open lid with an ignition source next to it turns a smelly service into the wrong kind of headline.

That haul container has no label and the lid isn't seated. An unlabeled container of grease waste sitting in a kitchen is a spill nobody can identify and a paperwork gap the hauler's manifest is supposed to close before it ever gets to this point.

title: Read the shift board
instruction: Check tonight's line assignment and who is running the flambé station.
rationale: The board tells you who is on the grill, who is on sauté, and whether flambé service is running tonight at all — a line cook stepping onto a station cold, not knowing whether an open flame is coming off it in twenty minutes, is exactly how a call of 'behind' arrives at somebody who wasn't expecting one.

title: Walk the line before service
instruction: Three things on this line are not right. Find them before the first ticket comes in.
rationale: Every one of these gets checked with your own eyes before service starts, because none of them look wrong from across the kitchen — a handle out, a wet towel and a missing drip pan are all things you only actually notice by walking the station, and by then it may already be somebody's hand.

title: Confirm the sauté pan is dry
instruction: Take the pan that's been wiped bone dry, not the one still beaded with rinse water.
rationale: A pan straight off the rack can still be carrying rinse water nobody would call wet from across the station — oil hitting even a few droplets of it spatters instantly, and it spatters toward whoever is standing over the pan pouring.

title: Heat the oil to shimmer, not smoke
instruction: Bring the oil up and commit once it's shimmering, before it starts smoking.
rationale: Shimmering oil is at temperature and ready for food; smoking oil is past its flash point and already breaking down, which is the difference between a sear and a flare the moment the protein hits the pan. The window between the two is short enough that this is read by watching the pan, not by guessing at a burner setting.

title: Carry the protein to the hot pan
instruction: Pick up the portioned tray and set it into the hot oil.
rationale: The protein goes into the pan the moment the oil is at temperature, not before and not a long minute after — held too long next to a pan that's already shimmering, it's oil breaking down for nothing, and dropped in too early it never sears at all.

title: Call it through the kitchen
instruction: Call "hot" pulling the sheet pan from the oven, then "behind" carrying it back through the aisle.
rationale: Nobody behind you can see a sheet pan coming out of an oven at shoulder height, and nobody in front of you can see you closing on their back — the two calls cover the two blind spots in order, the oven first and the aisle second, because that is the order your body actually moves through them.

title: Clear the flambé off the hood
instruction: Move the flambé pan onto the open flat-top space, clear of the baffle filters overhead.
rationale: Grease-laden filters sit right over the range for a reason that has nothing to do with a flambé — they exist to keep the duct clean, and an open flame reaching one of them lights the one thing in the room built out of accumulated fat. The pan moves to open space before it moves to fire.

title: Hold the flambé under control
instruction: Tilt the pan to the burner and hold the flame steady for the full count, clear of the hood.
rationale: A flambé's flame is controlled by the angle of the pan and how long it's held there, not by how dramatic it looks — held too long or tipped too far, the flame reaches higher than the cook standing over it planned for, over a station full of fabric and other people's hands.

title: Run the burn under cool water
instruction: Hold the burned hand under cool running water for the drill count.
rationale: The American Burn Association calls for cool — not cold, not iced — running water for a full twenty minutes, because that is how long it actually takes to carry heat out of the tissue below the skin's surface. This drill compresses the clock, but the standard it is teaching does not: on a real burn, the full twenty minutes is not optional.

title: Read the size and depth
instruction: Read the burn against the chart and commit once you've placed it correctly for the clinic decision.
rationale: OSHA's first-aid standard draws the line at how a burn is read, not how it feels: a small superficial burn is managed on-site, but anything partial-thickness larger than a few inches, or anything on the hand at all, is a clinic referral. Reading it correctly is what decides which of those two happens next.

title: Cover the burn, then refer it
